t: Chapter 25: A Wedding in Alabama
x: On February 10, 1939, a daughter was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts. Laurence gave the date and birthplace when he named his children in his American citizenship papers. Her name was Eugenie Elizabeth. There was an Eugenie on her mother’s side of the family, the Quebec-born grandmother whose name Constance herself carried. There was an Elizabeth on her father’s side, the woman who had raised him in Scotland. Both names that the little girl would carry in America were already familiar in her parents’ families. On Monday, October 9, Laurence and Constance married in Birmingham, Alabama. It was three days before her twenty-seventh birthday. He was thirty-two. At first glance there is very little in the places we knew them by that would lead anyone to Jefferson County. He had been born in Edinburgh and she in Providence. Their daughter had been born in Massachusetts. On the marriage application Laurence supplied a Chicago address for himself and a Providence one for his bride. His was 1860 South Hamlin Avenue. The following year the Chicago census would find his sister Janet and her husband Thomas Crombie at that address. The Providence address was 454 Broadway. For a couple standing on an Alabama record, the particulars reach a remarkable distance. One address takes us back to the sister who crossed the Atlantic with him. The other puts Constance in the city where I can follow her from the day she was born. The name on the groom’s line was Lawrence Douglas. He gave his occupation as salesman. The form asked who his parents were. Robert Douglas, he said, and Elizabeth McDonald. More than thirty years had gone by since Agnes Brown had stood as the mother on his Edinburgh birth entry. In Birmingham, the two people he chose to identify for his own marriage record were the man who had answered for him at school and the woman he had called his mother when he sailed. In the space for Constance’s parents he gave Albert B. Darcy and Eugenie Delaire. The bride’s name was entered as Constance Darcy. Laurence signed as the person supplying the particulars for them both. The page in the Jefferson County book holds more than the couple’s names. The application is where I find the addresses, the occupations and the names of the parents. The bond and the certificate are on the same page. It is the certificate that places the wedding itself in Birmingham on October 9. The distinction matters for a couple who gave home addresses in two other states. The Alabama marriage papers also identify the man who married Laurence and Constance. Thomas R. Lea was a municipal court judge. The certificate records his part in the ceremony and leaves the witness lines blank. Newspaper indexes place their names in two Birmingham papers the next day, the Post and the Age-Herald. Those newspaper references give us a place to look for how the city reported the event. The marriage record itself answers the question of when and by whom they were married. I have yet to learn why they chose Birmingham. Six months later they were keeping house together on Valencia Street in San Francisco, with a one-year-old daughter born in Massachusetts. When Laurence was asked about his marriage again in Pennsylvania, he gave the bride’s family name, Darcy, and once again he supplied October 9, 1939, and Birmingham. That is how a single day in Alabama became part of the story of the family my mother grew up in. Jefferson County marriage license record, book 154, page 409 Lawrence Douglas and Constance Darcy. t: Chapter 26: San Francisco
x: By the spring of 1940, Laurence and Constance had crossed the country and come to San Francisco. In April 1940 their home was in the Mission District. The census page records Valencia Street. On their line the space for the house number is empty. I can take the family to that street in the spring of 1940 and put a figure on the rent they paid there. On April 11, 1940, a census taker came to Valencia Street in the Mission. The Douglas family paid thirty-three dollars a month in rent. Laurence worked in a clothing store. The words used for his trade were window trimmer. He had worked forty-eight hours in the week the census asked about. For the whole of the previous year he reported earnings of two thousand two hundred and forty dollars. The census asked where each person had lived five years earlier. For Laurence the answer was Chicago. For Constance it was Providence. Their daughter was one year old. The three birthplaces in the household were Scotland, Rhode Island and Massachusetts. Now the three of them lived in California. His employer was Bond Stores, one of the largest men's clothing chains in America, founded in Cleveland in 1914. The San Francisco store stood at Post and Kearny streets, two blocks from Union Square. The 1941 city directory lists him as a displayman at Bond Clothes, with his wife Constance. In Europe the war went on. France fell that summer, and London was bombed through the autumn. The United States had yet to enter the war. Even so, on October 16, 1940, Laurence registered for the draft. The reverse of his card carries the stamp of Local Board 94. He gave a new address, 129 Julian Avenue. He named his employer, Bond Stores, at Post and Kearny. For the person who would always know where to reach him, he gave his wife, Constance. The card describes him as about six feet tall and 160 pounds, with blue eyes, and he signed it Laurence Brown Douglas. It was in San Francisco that my mother was born. Her parents called her Constance Anderson Douglas. She had her mother's first name. Anderson was the name Laurence had used for Lizzie at the Canadian border. My mother's birthday is February 2. California's birth index gives the year as 1941. In his citizenship papers her father subsequently gave 1942. The month and day agree. For the year I have followed the California birth index. In June 1941 Laurence and his wife went north into Canada. He had obtained a re-entry permit for the trip. On Saturday, June 21, they returned by motor coach at Blaine, Washington. The inspector put down his occupation as displayman, his age, his height of about six feet, his brown hair and blue eyes, and their San Francisco address on Mirabel Avenue. Brown is the description on this card. The one at Detroit had said fair. It was nearly twelve years since Laurence had first entered the country at Detroit with fifty dollars and the name of a brother-in-law in Chicago. Now he gave an address on the Pacific coast, and Constance was beside him. The next day, Germany invaded the Soviet Union. Six months later, the war would reach America. t: Chapter 27: The Night of the Sirens
x: The last time I can put my grandparents together before America entered the war is on a border card. On June 21, 1941, Laurence returned to the United States at Blaine, Washington. The card says his wife Constance, an American citizen, was with him. Their destination was San Francisco. My family remembers a different arrangement by autumn. Laurence had gone east to the Pittsburgh district for work, and Constance was still in San Francisco. Two men in Pennsylvania left a date that helps us follow the family account. David Hunter was a machinist and Frank Holliday a clerk. Each later swore that he had known my grandfather since September 1941. There were people who could account for him on the West Coast, too. When he applied for citizenship, the period for which the authorities sought evidence from San Francisco ran from February to September of that year. Across those papers and the family’s memory, September is the month that keeps coming back. On Sunday, December 7, the first reports of the attack on Pearl Harbor reached San Francisco at about half past eleven in the morning. By one that afternoon people were volunteering at police and fire stations. At the Northern Police Station on Greenwich Street, 385 had lined up by half past three. The city needed to know what each could do. One volunteer, Hazel Shive, said she could drive a truck or work as a nurse. It is her name and her offer that survive in the newspaper account of that afternoon. The alarms in San Francisco itself came the following day. At about a quarter past six on Monday evening, people began to hear warnings. Police cars sounded their sirens. Fire engines added theirs. A blackout required the people who could see a light to find somebody who could actually turn it off. Some of the hardest to extinguish were electric advertising signs on rooftops. They had been set on timers, and their controls were out of reach of the people below. David Perlman was a young Chronicle reporter that December. Sent up to the roof of the newspaper building with binoculars, he saw a light in the sky and thought he had spotted a plane. It was a star. The newspaper’s front page the next morning counted four alarms. People in the streets on Monday evening had to decide what to do with the information available then. No bombs fell on San Francisco that night. I have my family’s account of where my grandparents were that autumn. It does not give me a house in which to put Constance on December 8, or tell me when she and Laurence heard from one another. The city’s newspapers preserve the hours of the alarms, the places where people volunteered and even the mistake a reporter made on a roof. My grandmother’s whereabouts that Monday evening belong to her own, unrecorded part of the story. The next address I can give for all four of them is 612 California Avenue. In spite of its name, the street was in Avalon, Pennsylvania, outside Pittsburgh. On February 11, 1943, Laurence listed Constance Darcy as his wife and gave the names of the two little girls living there, Eugenie Elizabeth and Constance Anderson. The younger girl was my mother. Her family remembered her parents in two different cities in the autumn of 1941. By February 1943 her father could give one address for them all. t: Chapter 28: An American Citizen
x: Laurence Brown Douglas was living at 612 California Avenue in Avalon, just outside Pittsburgh, when he petitioned for American citizenship. He was a display manager for Bond Stores. The papers describe him as five feet eleven, with blue eyes and brown hair. They give his date of birth as June 14, 1907. More than thirty-five years after Agnes registered him in Edinburgh, her son was giving the same date for himself in Pennsylvania. His petition was numbered 139903. One of the questions took him back to his entrance into the country. He gave Detroit and September 15, 1929. The card made at Detroit survives. The younger man on it was single, with fifty dollars and a brother-in-law in Chicago. The man making the petition in Pennsylvania had a wife and children and a job with Bond Stores. He gave the authorities enough particulars to put the two records together. Two men in the Pittsburgh area vouched for him on February 11, 1943. David Hunter was a machinist. Frank Holliday was a clerk. On March 3, two people who had known him in California gave depositions in San Francisco. Their names were William Howard Vahlkamp and Betty Johnstone Sherwood. His move across the country meant that some of the people able to speak for him lived more than two thousand miles away. The California witnesses had known him in the city where he worked before moving east. Their depositions still belong to the same file as the evidence given in Pittsburgh. His neighbors and acquaintances had a part in the record he left my mother. They could speak about the months in which they saw him. His account of his birth, his marriage and the births of his daughters was his own. He named his wife, Constance Darcy, and gave Birmingham as the place of their marriage. He listed Eugenie Elizabeth and Constance Anderson as his daughters. He also gave the date on which he had entered the United States at Detroit and the name he had used on entry. Lawrence Brown. On May 6, 1943, he took the oath and was admitted as a citizen of the United States. On the record of that day his name is Laurence Brown Douglas. February 11 was the date of the petition and the Pittsburgh witnesses. March 3 was the date of the California testimony. The day he became a citizen was the Thursday in May. It is one of the reasons I can tell my mother with confidence that the boy registered in Edinburgh, the young grocer who came through Detroit, and the man who raised her were the same person. On the citizenship papers he brought the names together himself. Citizenship file 139903, Western District of Pennsylvania Pittsburgh witnesses, February 11, 1943. t: Chapter 29: River Avenue
x: By 1947 the family was back in Rhode Island. The Pawtucket directory gives their address as 97 Magill Street. Laurence was dressing windows. In Providence by 1950, he and Constance were living at 148 General Street. They remained in the directories there for several years. The 1956 Providence directory lists them at 644 River Avenue. Laurence and Constance rented the house on River Avenue, as they did every home they lived in together. Constance is named beside him in the Pawtucket directory. The shift from Magill Street to General Street is one I can trace in city books whose compilers were simply keeping track of the people who lived and worked among their customers. Entries survive for the years in which an American census would leave us waiting a decade. Those entries help me place the girls’ childhood on three streets, first Magill in Pawtucket, then General and River in Providence. Eugenie Elizabeth, Constance Anderson and Norma were the three Douglas girls. Their father's work took him into stores around Pawtucket. It is easier now to find an address where he worked than a photograph of a window he dressed. A store could change its windows every season. The family kept a clearer picture of the man. He was quiet. He loved to read. They remembered how particular he was about his appearance, right down to his hair. While the girls were growing up, their mother's family was nearby. In October 1954 her brother, Albert Norman Darcy, died at thirty-eight. Their father, Albert Blake Darcy, the newspaper linotype operator, died in 1957. Janet and Thomas were still in Illinois. Both had become American citizens too, Thomas in 1947 and Janet the following spring. As in the marriage papers, the family is spread over more than one city. Lizzie appears with the Crombies in the 1940 Chicago census. In Rhode Island one can follow Constance’s Darcy family in directories, draft cards, newspaper notices and the cemetery records in Cranston and Pawtucket. The records fill in different parts of the family table. My mother’s own recollections supply the man at the head of it. The directory for 1960 names one of the shops where Laurence worked, Carter’s Men Store in Pawtucket. The next directory gives his business in two words, window displays, and prints 644 River Avenue as the address. By the end of his life he was working for himself. Beside him in the directory is Constance, a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital. She had trained at the Rhode Island School of Practical Nursing. I first came across the two of them in separate entries in a Providence directory, a hairdresser on Westminster and a display manager on Weybosset. Almost a quarter of a century later, the directory lists them together at their home on River Avenue and gives a separate place of work for Constance. t: Chapter 30: The Ninth of March
x: On Thursday, March 9, 1961, Laurence Brown Douglas died at St. Joseph’s Hospital in Providence. He was fifty-three. My mother remembered how little warning the family had. They understood the illness to be lung cancer. The newspaper described it as a brief illness. I have her account and the newspaper, and each tells the part its author knew. At the time of his death, Laurence and Constance were renting the house at 644 River Avenue. The city directory listed his window-display business there and his wife, Constance, as a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital. The woman who had begun her working life dressing hair was nursing by then. The display man who once worked for a national chain was working for himself. The weather station at T. F. Green Airport in Warwick recorded rain, fog, sleet and snow for March 9. Temperatures ranged from thirty-one to forty-two degrees Fahrenheit. Those are observations from the airport, a few miles south of the city. His Scottish birth register gives an hour. The obituary gives a day for his death, and that is as closely as I can place it. On Saturday, the Pawtucket Times printed his obituary on page three. It said he had been born in Edinburgh, Scotland. It said he was the son of the late Robert and Elizabeth (Anderson) Douglas. It said he had worked for the Bond Clothing Company, and had his own display business, and that for the past fifteen years he had dressed windows for Pawtucket firms. It named his wife, Constance, their daughters, and his sister, Mrs. Thomas Crombie of Chicago. The paper also gave the arrangements being made for Monday, March 13. The announced hour was ten in the morning at the Ruth E. Urquhart funeral home, 812 Greenwich Avenue in Warwick. There is a difference between an invitation in a Saturday newspaper and a family memory of who came through the door on Monday. The address and hour are in print. The people in the room are beyond my telling. The newspaper gave the facts of a working life. The family remembered other things. His friends called him Doug. He was always impeccably dressed, his hair perfectly combed. He was quiet. He loved to read. The Edinburgh register preserves his mother’s name, Agnes Brown. The Rhode Island obituary preserves the names of the people who raised him, Robert and Elizabeth Douglas. His American citizenship papers bring the two families together in the name he used for himself, Laurence Brown Douglas. That is the name I wanted my mother to have on the cover of her father’s book. t: Epilogue: The Names He Carried
x: After Laurence died, Nan went on nursing. The 1963 Warwick directory calls her the widow of Lawrence B. Douglas. It gives her occupation as nurse and her home address as 119 Phillips Avenue. By the time her grandchildren knew her, the watch that had come from Scotland was still in the family. That is the part of its travels I can tell from my own life. Constance’s obituary remembers her practical-nursing training and eight years at Cranston General Hospital. She retired in 1974. In later life she lived on Sixth Street in East Greenwich and belonged to St. Francis de Sales parish. She died on April 12, 1994, at eighty-one. The Catholic cemetery index places her at Saint Ann in Cranston, in section 5, lot 84. That is a place a grandchild can find. Janet, the older sister who had left Dunfermline before him, survived him too. The Social Security death index gives December 1979 and a last residence in Maywood, Illinois. She was seventy-nine. In 1940 Lizzie, under the name Elizabeth Anderson, had been counted in Janet’s Chicago household. Twenty-one years later the Rhode Island obituary spoke of both Robert and Elizabeth as deceased. Her final address and the date of her death are particulars I still hope to put beside her name. Agnes Brown had married Thomas McKenzie in Edinburgh. His Army paper keeps the birthdays of their daughters Mary and Jean. My grandfather had two younger sisters through his birth mother and an older sister, Janet, through the family who raised him. I know a great deal about the bond with Janet because the two of them kept turning up in the same places. I do not know whether he and the McKenzie girls ever met. I set out to give my grandfather a voice. But more than that, I did it for his daughter, my mother, Constance Douglas, who is eighty-five as I write this. She remembered her father too, and when she spoke of him there was always a little more sadness in it than I ever heard from Nan. I wanted to give him back to her, to make his life real and tangible again. When I began, a single word inside a watch seemed a small thing to go on. Now the same city appears on a birth register signed by Agnes, on a census that calls her child Lizzie’s son, and on the American papers in which he told his own story. We have the names of the people who answered for him as a boy and the names he gave when it was his turn to answer. We have a photograph of him standing beside his sister, each of them with ice cream. That is a family I can introduce to my mother. The watch is on my desk as I write this. I can open the case as Nan opened it for me. The engraving still reads Edinburgh. Sources and record notes Janet Crombie, Social Security Death Index. December 1979, last residence Maywood. t: Appendix: A Chronology of His Life
x: June 14, 1907 Agnes gives birth to Lawrence Brown in Edinburgh. July 4, 1907 Agnes registers her son’s birth. April 2, 1911 The census places Laurence B. with Elizabeth and Janet Douglas. August 19, 1912 Lawrence Douglas enters Queen Anne Infant School. June 19, 1921 At fourteen, he is a grocer’s message boy in Dunfermline. September 1929 He sails with Janet from Greenock, reaches Quebec and is admitted at Detroit. Spring 1930 The Chicago census records him with the Crombies. 1937–1938 Providence directories list a display manager on Weybosset Street. October 9, 1939 Laurence and Constance marry in Birmingham, Alabama. April 1940 The census records their household on Valencia Street in San Francisco. May 6, 1943 Laurence Brown Douglas becomes a United States citizen. 1956 The Providence directory lists the family at 644 River Avenue. March 9, 1961 Laurence dies in Providence.

t: Laurence Brown Douglas
x: Laurence Brown Douglas 1907–1961 Laurence Brown Douglas is the man at the center of this book. He was born at nine o'clock on the evening of June 14, 1907, at the Royal Maternity Hospital in Lauriston Place, Edinburgh. Twenty days later his mother, Agnes Brown, registered him as Lawrence Brown. For her home she gave Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar. By the spring of 1911 he was living at 16 Lochrin Place in Edinburgh as Laurence B. Douglas, the son of the house of Robert and Elizabeth Douglas. In 1912 the family moved to Dunfermline. He grew up there with the Douglases' daughter, Janet. Robert Douglas died of tuberculosis in 1919, and in October 1920, at thirteen, Laurence left school with an exemption and went to work as a message boy for a grocer. In September 1929 he sailed from Greenock with Janet on the Duchess of Bedford and crossed into the United States at Detroit as Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, grocer, six feet tall, fair hair, blue eyes, fifty dollars. In Chicago he lived with Janet and her husband. By 1937 he was in Providence as a display man, dressing store windows on Weybosset Street, the trade he would follow for the rest of his life. In October 1939 he married Constance Eugenie Darcy in Birmingham, Alabama. They lived in San Francisco, where he dressed the windows of Bond Stores, and in 1943, in a federal court in Pittsburgh, he became an American citizen as Laurence Brown Douglas: both names at once. After the war the family settled in Pawtucket and then Providence, at 644 River Avenue. He died at St. Joseph's Hospital in Providence on March 9, 1961, at fifty-three, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston. His grandson, Doug Garceau, wrote this book. t: Agnes McGarth Brown
x: Agnes McGarth Brown born 1885 Agnes McGarth Brown was Laurence's mother. She was born at half past two in the afternoon on December 18, 1885, in a ploughman's cottage at Edston, near Peebles, the second daughter of George Brown and Christina Henderson. Her father gave her his own mother's name, Agnes McGarth. He died when she was three and a half months old, and her mother took the two girls home to Libberton parish, to the row of cottages at Quothquan. Her mother died in February 1891, when Agnes was five, and her grandmother, Jane Henderson, took her in. That June her grandmother died too. Agnes grew up in the cottage later called Lime Tree, with her sister Mary, her uncle Andrew Henderson and James Parker, the boy her grandmother had raised. A few doors along lived Mary Archibald, whose brother Alexander would become the gardener at Shieldhill House. By 1907 Agnes was a domestic servant. On July 4, 1907, she registered her son, Lawrence Brown, in Edinburgh and gave her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill. In the 1901 census a similar cottage address was associated with Mary Archibald. Their household arrangements in 1906–07 remain unknown. By 1911 she was a nurse at the Royal Edinburgh Asylum in Morningside. On August 28, 1911, she married an asylum attendant, Thomas McKay McKenzie, by declaration at Chambers Street, before the same registrar who had recorded her son's birth. They had two daughters, Mary Christina in 1912 and Jean Henderson in 1914. One portrait of her is known. Where and when she died has not yet been found. x: George Brown 1862–1886 George Brown was Laurence's grandfather, the father of Agnes. He was born on July 18, 1862 (a date from other researchers’ family trees), one of at least ten children of William Brown, a ploughman, and Agnes McGarth, and he became a ploughman like his father. He registered her himself on the last day of the year and signed as her father. x: William Brown born about 1835 William Brown was Laurence's great-grandfather on his mother's side. He was a ploughman in the sheep country of Peeblesshire, born about 1835, who walked behind a pair of horses turning the ground for oats and turnips and moved from farm to farm as the term days dictated. Like most farm laborers of his time, he owned no land and no house; the cottage came with the job. He married Agnes McGarth of Tweedsmuir. They had at least ten children: William, about 1859; Lawrence Tweedie, 1860; George, 1862; then Alexander, Jane, John, James Tweedie, Agnes, Thomas and Tweedie McGarth Brown. t: Sir Nathaniel Dunlop
x: Sir Nathaniel Dunlop 1830–1919 Nathaniel Dunlop owned the Shieldhill estate when Laurence was born. He was born at Campbeltown on April 7, 1830, served the Allan Line, the Glasgow shipping company whose steamers carried tens of thousands of Scottish emigrants to Canada, for half a century, and was chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust. In 1898 he bought Shieldhill from the Chancellor family, and with it the village of Quothquan and its cottages. He rebuilt houses in the village, and in 1903 he and his daughter, Ellen, put up Shieldhill Hall for evening services. He had been a widower since 1867. On June 28, 1907, his name was in the King's birthday honours, and on July 15 he was knighted at Buckingham Palace as Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill, Biggar. In the newspapers of those years: on May 4, 1906, the Motherwell Times reported his application, as Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill, Biggar, for a water supply to the houses he owned at Quothquan. In April 1907 the Hamilton Advertiser's Biggar column noted him at a ceremony in Glasgow. On June 6, 1907, eight days before Laurence was born, The Scotsman carried an advertisement for leases on the Shieldhill Estate. On June 28, 1907, the Morning Post's list of new knights described him as residing at Shieldhill, Biggar, a justice of the peace for Lanarkshire and for Glasgow. (Sources: British Newspaper Archive.) He was called Doctor in print. The University of Glasgow made him an honorary Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) at its graduation ceremony on Tuesday, April 23, 1907, in the presence of the Prince and Princess of Wales, as the Hamilton Advertiser's Biggar column reported on April 27. Before that, the papers called him Mr Nathaniel Dunlop. From then on, newspapers named him "Dr. Nathaniel Dunlop": the Naval & Military Record of June 6, 1907, listing guests at the King's turbine yacht; the Daily Record of June 22, 1907, quoting his speech aboard the Marmion; and the Liverpool Journal of Commerce of October 24, 1907, as chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust. (Source: British Newspaper Archive.) He died at Shieldhill on November 15, 1919. His will names his daughter, nephews and nieces, his household staff and charities. Estate owner Wife Died 1867 Daughter Ellen Dunlop

t: Ellen Dunlop
x: Ellen Dunlop 1867–1958 Ellen Smith Dunlop was the only child of Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill. Her mother died within weeks of her birth, and she became her father's constant companion. She never married. In 1903 she and her father built Shieldhill Hall in Quothquan for evening worship and winter lectures. At her death in 1958 it passed to the Church of Scotland. A shrewd manager, she financed the Thankerton Creamery in 1911, the first in Lanarkshire, partly to spare farm wives and servants the drudgery of hand dairying. She helped found the Quothquan Women's Rural Institute in 1918, bred prize Highland cattle and fed the garden birds every day. The papers kept track of the hall. On April 13, 1912, the Hamilton Advertiser's Quothquan column reported an amateur concert held in Shieldhill Hall. On November 16, 1918, the same column reported that on Thursday, November 7, a meeting in Shieldhill Hall, Quothquan, addressed by Miss Nannie Brown of the Board of Agriculture and Miss E. B. Mitchell of Langlees, Biggar, voted unanimously to form a Women's Rural Institute in Quothquan, with 31 members. (Source: British Newspaper Archive.) She ran Shieldhill herself after 1919 and died in 1958, aged 89, leaving much of her estate to her staff, above all her maid and companion of fifty years. Owner's daughter Father Sir Nathaniel Dunlop

t: Shieldhill Estate and House
x: Shieldhill Estate and House the big house above Quothquan Shieldhill was the estate on the hill above the village of Quothquan, in the parish of Libberton in Upper Clydesdale, four miles from Biggar. Its house was a rambling mansion built around an old tower, with stonework of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and additions of about 1820. Below the house lay the village of Quothquan, with the row the census of 1891 called Castle, where Agnes Brown grew up. The Chancellor family held the lands of Shieldhill from 1434, when George Chancellor was granted them with part of Quothquan. Shieldhill became the family's main home after their house at Quothquan was destroyed, following William Chancellor's support for Mary Queen of Scots at the Battle of Langside. The family buried their dead in the ruined old kirk at Quothquan, which they had taken as a family burial place around 1780. In 1898 they sold Shieldhill to Nathaniel Dunlop, a Glasgow shipowner of the Allan Line. Dunlop rebuilt Huntfield Place, turning six houses into four, enlarged the smith's house, and in 1903, with his daughter, Ellen, put up Shieldhill Hall in the village for evening services. On census night in 1901 Alexander Archibald, his wife Annie and Susan Cumisky were enumerated at “Shieldhill.” Their precise building is unrecorded. Below the house, Mary Archibald lived at Gean Tree Cottages and fifteen-year-old Agnes Brown lived at Lime Tree Cottage. Shieldhill is the place at the center of Laurence's beginning. When Agnes registered her son in Edinburgh in July 1907, she gave her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar. The house is still there, a category B listed building whose oldest surviving part is a sixteenth-century square keep. It became a country house hotel in 1959 and reopened in August 2020 after a long refurbishment. In 1997 Nelson Mandela stayed there during the Commonwealth summit in Edinburgh and planted an oak tree in the grounds. t: Robert Douglas
x: Robert Douglas 1876–1919 Robert Douglas was the man who raised Laurence. He was born at 9 Canon Street, Edinburgh, on May 8, 1876, the son of Archibald Douglas, then a traveller for a wood merchant and later a forester, and Isabella Gray. On June 9, 1899, at twenty-three, a saw miller, he married Elizabeth Millar McDonald at 34 St Patrick Square by the forms of the Free Church of Scotland. Within two years he was a stone machineman, a skilled worker who cut and dressed stone by machine. Their daughter, Janet Page Douglas, was born on April 29, 1900. Family information says a second daughter, Isabella Gray Douglas, died as an infant. By April 1911 the boy born Lawrence Brown was living in their home at 16 Lochrin Place as Laurence B. Douglas, their son. In 1912 the family moved to Dunfermline, and the school register named Robert as the boy's guardian. His death register gives the cause as pulmonary tuberculosis, and records lupus since childhood. He died at Woodburn Sanatorium in Morningside, Edinburgh, on September 9, 1919, aged forty-three. Laurence was twelve. t: Elizabeth Miller McDonald (Lizzie Douglas)
x: Elizabeth Miller McDonald (Lizzie Douglas) born 1874 Elizabeth Millar McDonald, known as Lizzie, was the woman who raised Laurence, and the mother he named when he sailed for America. She was born at Liberton, on the southern edge of Edinburgh, on May 31, 1874. Her mother, Ann McDonald, was about twenty. Ann married Robert Alexander Hope on July 28, 1876, and in 1878 they sailed for New Zealand, leaving Lizzie, four, with her grandparents, John and Janet McDonald, at Gilmerton. The dates of the marriage and the sailing come from family trees compiled by other researchers. She went into service at sixteen. On June 9, 1899, she married Robert Douglas, a saw miller, and for her own parents she gave the names of the grandparents who had raised her. Their daughter Janet was born in 1900. By 1911 she was raising the boy born Lawrence Brown as her son, Laurence B. Douglas, at 16 Lochrin Place. A woman who had been taken in took in a child. Widowed in 1919, she worked as a school cleaner in Dunfermline. By 1929 she was using the surname Anderson, Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson of 39 Grieve Street, and both Janet and Laurence named her as their mother when they sailed for America. In September 1934, at sixty, she followed them. She sailed on the Letitia to Quebec and on October 2 entered the United States at Port Huron, Michigan, to live with Janet at 1518 Kostner Avenue in Chicago. The woman who raised him Mother Ann McDonald (later Ann Hope) Father Not recorded Raised by John and Janet McDonald, her grandparents Husband Robert Douglas, married 1899 Children Janet Page Douglas, 1900; Isabella Gray Douglas, died as an infant (family information) Raised Laurence Brown Douglas

t: Ann McDonald Hope
x: Ann McDonald Hope about 1854–1915 Ann McDonald was the mother of Elizabeth (Lizzie) McDonald, the woman who raised Laurence. She was about twenty when Lizzie was born at Liberton in 1874. On July 28, 1876, she married Robert Alexander Hope, a laborer, at 33 Regent Park Square in Glasgow. In 1878 Ann and Robert Hope sailed for New Zealand on assisted passages. Their son, John Rakaia Hope, was born at sea on September 26, 1878, and named for the emigrant ship. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa and raised four more children. Lizzie, four, stayed behind with her grandparents. Ann died at Cross Creek on January 13, 1915. These details come from family trees compiled by other researchers. t: Robert Alexander Hope
x: Robert Alexander Hope 1852–1930 Robert Alexander Hope married Ann McDonald, the mother of Lizzie Douglas, in Glasgow on July 28, 1876. He was born at Rigg, near Gretna, on July 14, 1852, the son of Gavin Hope and Elizabeth Millar. In 1878 he and Ann emigrated to New Zealand, where their son John Rakaia Hope was born at sea. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa. Robert died at Pukekohe on December 3, 1930. Lizzie stayed behind in Scotland with her grandparents. t: John and Janet McDonald
x: John and Janet McDonald born about 1829 John McDonald and his wife, Janet, born Janet Page, raised their granddaughter Lizzie, the woman who would raise Laurence. In 1881 the census found them on the Main Road at Gilmerton, south of Edinburgh, in the country of coal pits and miners' rows: John, fifty-two; Janet, fifty-two; their son George; a daughter, Janet; a son, Alexander; and Elizabeth, six, entered as Grandchild. When Lizzie married Robert Douglas in 1899, she gave their names as her parents: John McDonald, coal salesman, and Janet McDonald, born Page. She named her first daughter Janet Page Douglas, after the grandmother who had raised her. t: Archibald Douglas and Isabella Gray
x: Archibald Douglas and Isabella Gray married 1863 Archibald Douglas and Isabella Gray were the parents of Robert Douglas, the man who raised Laurence. They married in January 1863 in the parish of Newton, on the southeastern edge of Edinburgh. When Robert was born in 1876 at 9 Canon Street, Archibald was a traveller for a wood merchant; by 1899 he was a forester. Their names appear in Robert's birth, marriage and death entries. t: Janet Page Douglas Crombie
x: Janet Page Douglas Crombie 1900–1979 Janet Page Douglas was the daughter of Robert and Lizzie Douglas, and the sister Laurence grew up with. She was born in Edinburgh on April 29, 1900, seven years before him. In 1911 they were in the same house at Lochrin Place, and in August 1912 the Queen Anne School in Dunfermline admitted them two days apart from the same address. She left school at fourteen in August 1914, and in 1921 she was a clerkess with the Dunfermline Co-operative Society. On July 16, 1926, she married Thomas Crombie, and that September they crossed into the United States at Detroit and settled on South Kostner Avenue in Chicago. In May 1929 she came home to Dunfermline, and in September she sailed back with Laurence on the Duchess of Bedford. The 1930 census found him in her household. In 1936 Janet had twin daughters, Betty and Jessie. She became an American citizen in 1948 and died in December 1979, her last home Maywood, Illinois. Sister Father Robert Douglas Mother Elizabeth Millar McDonald (Lizzie Douglas) Raised alongside Laurence Brown Douglas Husband Thomas Crombie, married 1926 Children Elizabeth (Betty) and Jessie Crombie, twins, 1936

t: Thomas Crombie
x: Thomas Crombie born about 1894 Thomas Crombie was the husband of Janet Douglas, Laurence's sister. He was a man from Kinross, thirty-two when they married in Dunfermline on July 16, 1926. That September they crossed into the United States at Detroit and settled on the West Side of Chicago. When Laurence arrived in 1929, he named Thomas, his brother-in-law, at 1534 South Kostner Avenue, as the person he was going to. On the 1930 census Thomas was the head of the house, a furniture salesman, with Laurence entered as his brother-in-law. He became an American citizen on September 9, 1947. Brother-in-law Wife Janet Page Douglas, married 1926 Children Elizabeth (Betty) and Jessie Crombie, twins, 1936

t: Betty and Jessie Crombie
x: Betty and Jessie Crombie 1936–2009 and 1936–2015 Elizabeth and Jessie Crombie were twin daughters of Janet and Thomas Crombie, born in Chicago on October 3, 1936. Elizabeth was called Betty. Their uncle Laurence was twenty-nine. Jessie married Ronald H. Power in Cook County in September 1958. Betty died in Minneapolis on June 23, 2009, and Jessie at Poplar Grove, Illinois, on December 12, 2015. Nieces Father Thomas Crombie Mother Janet Page Douglas Crombie Uncle Laurence Brown Douglas

t: Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas
x: Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas 1912–1994 Constance Eugenie Darcy was Laurence's wife for twenty-one years. She was born on Saturday, October 12, 1912, at 410 Smith Street, Providence, the first child of Albert Blake Darcy, a printer, and Eugenie Emma Delaire. Her parents later divorced, and she grew up between their households. She trained as a hairdresser, and in 1937 and 1938 she worked on Westminster Street, a block from Laurence's work on Weybosset Street. On October 9, 1939, she and Laurence were married in Birmingham, Alabama. They lived in San Francisco, where he dressed windows for Bond Stores, then in the Pittsburgh district, and after the war in Pawtucket and Providence. She trained at the Rhode Island School of Practical Nursing, and by 1961 she was a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital. Laurence died in 1961, when she was forty-eight. She kept nursing, worked eight years at Cranston General Hospital, and retired in 1974. In her last years she lived in East Greenwich. The family remembers her pleasant, congenial nature. She died on April 12, 1994, and was buried with Laurence at Saint Ann Cemetery, Cranston. Wife Father Albert Blake Darcy Mother Eugenie Emma Delaire Brother Albert Norman Darcy Husband Laurence Brown Douglas, married 1939 Children Three daughters: Eugenie, the eldest; Constance; and Norma, the youngest

t: Albert Blake Darcy
x: Albert Blake Darcy 1888–1957 Albert Blake Darcy was the father of Constance, Laurence's wife. He was born on November 20, 1888, at Rumford, in East Providence, the first child of John F. and Maggie Darcy, whose family had come from Ireland. By 1910, at twenty-one, he was an apprentice on a Monotype machine, learning to set type. On January 16, 1912, he married Eugenie Emma Delaire, seventeen. Their daughter Constance was born that October, and their son Albert Norman in 1915. He moved where the work was, to Boston and Taunton and back to Providence, where he set type for the Pawtucket Times and later the Providence Journal. The marriage ended in divorce; on August 1, 1929, he took out a marriage license in Brooklyn, New York, to marry Theresa B. Sullivan, and settled at Shawomet, in Warwick. In 1950 the census found him at 60 West Shore Road, Warwick, with Theresa, still a linotype operator in newspaper publishing. His mother, Margaret Jane Darcy, died at his house there in 1942. He died on November 4, 1957, sixteen days short of his sixty-ninth birthday, and was buried at Mount Saint Mary Cemetery in Pawtucket. Father-in-law Father John F. Darcy Mother Margaret Jane (Maggie) Darcy First wife Eugenie Emma Delaire, married 1912 Second wife Theresa B. Sullivan, license Brooklyn, 1929 Children Constance Eugenie, 1912; Albert Norman, 1915

t: Eugenie Emma Delaire Darcy
x: Eugenie Emma Delaire Darcy 1894–1966 Eugenie Emma Delaire was the mother of Constance, Laurence's wife. She was born at Sutton, Quebec, the daughter of Timothy and Julia Delaire, one of the many French Canadian families who came down to New England. She married Albert Blake Darcy in Providence on January 16, 1912, at seventeen. Her widowed mother, Julia, boarded with them on Smith Street the next year. By 1930 she was divorced, the head of her own household at 111 Pratt Street, working as an interior decorator at a rug works. In the mid-1930s she and Constance shared a home, at Abbott Street and then Dartmouth Avenue. She died in 1966 and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston. Mother-in-law Father Timothy Delaire Mother Julia Delaire Husband Albert Blake Darcy, married 1912 Children Constance Eugenie, 1912; Albert Norman, 1915

t: Albert Norman Darcy
x: Albert Norman Darcy 1915–1954 Albert Norman Darcy was the younger brother of Constance, Laurence's wife. He was born at Taunton, Massachusetts, on December 7, 1915. On October 16, 1940, the same day Laurence registered for the draft in San Francisco, Albert signed his own draft card in Warwick, Rhode Island, and named his wife, Claire. He died on October 1, 1954, aged thirty-eight, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston, in section 5, lot 84. Laurence was buried in the same lot in 1961. t: Records of Laurence Brown Douglas (1907–1961): Finding Aid
x: Collection summary Title Records of Laurence Brown Douglas (1907–1961) and his family Dates 1848–1961 (bulk 1885–1961) Extent 100 documents; 164 catalogued details not used in the book Compiler Doug Garceau, grandson of Laurence Brown Douglas Languages English Companion work The Names He Carried: The Laurence Brown Douglas Story, 1907 to 1961 Scope and content The collection documents the birth of Lawrence Brown at the Royal Maternity Hospital, Edinburgh, on 14 June 1907; his mother Agnes Brown and her family in Peeblesshire and Lanarkshire; the Douglas household that raised him in Edinburgh and Dunfermline; the Shieldhill estate and the Dunlop family; his emigration to the United States in 1929; and his life in Chicago, San Francisco, Pittsburgh and Rhode Island until his death in 1961. Arrangement Documents are arranged in nine series by record type, and within each series by date. Each document has a permanent catalog number (DOC-001 to DOC-100) matching its Cold Case File item number. Series 1. Civil registration (births, marriages, deaths) (19 documents) Series 2. Directories and electoral rolls (13 documents) Series 6. Probate, wills and reference works (9 documents) Series 7. Newspapers and obituaries (4 documents) Series 8. School records (1 documents) Series 9. Each scanned page carries "Digitized by Google" at the foot.] [Page 280] 280 Obituary. It is owing, on the other hand, to the absence in the child-mind of both the inertia of rest and the inertia of movement that it exhibits such a high degree of suggestibility. The child-mind maintains for so short a time and in so slight a fashion any one course of action or set purpose, that almost any fresh idea—"suggestion"—from parent or playmate can turn it aside into a fresh channel, and that, in turn, can be easily supplanted by some other, newer still. There is so little mental inertia of rest belonging to the idea in possession of the mind that it can be easily supplanted, and the new idea has so little "momentum" that it can be easily turned out of its course for some new thing. Thus, a "volatile nature" is one with but slight mental functional inertia of movement; a "dogged temperament" is one with much. The great obstinacy of the uncultured, and the "fixed delusion" of the lunatic, are cases of pathologically developed psychic inertia of rest. [Double rule] Obituary. [in Gothic lettering] JAMES DUNLOP, M.D. DR. JAMES DUNLOP died, at the age of 67, at his house, 16 Carlton Place, Glasgow, on Wednesday, 13th March, 1901. By his death a well-known figure is removed from the ranks of the medical profession of Glasgow. Up till a few years ago, when failing health compelled him to give up a large portion of his work, he was one of the busiest men in the City, his public engagements being numerous and his private practice extensive. Of a genial and kindly disposition, Dr. Dunlop was much esteemed by all who came into contact with him. He was a most approachable man, who was at all times willing to do his best for those who sought his advice in cases of delicacy or difficulty. Possessed of a fund of humour and anecdote, his conversation was always interesting, and as a travelling companion he was delightful, wiling away the hours of a long journey with his vivacity and racy talk. We will not readily forget the pleasure we enjoyed in his society during a visit to Rome, when the International Medical Congress met in the Eternal City in 1894. Though even then in somewhat feeble health, his enthusiasm was great, his [Page 281] Obituary. 281 energy untiring, and his interest in the antiquities of Rome intense. All busy medical men have, or should have, a hobby or relaxation, which, on occasion, may take their minds away from the monotonous daily routine of professional work. Dr. Dunlop had two—the study of natural history, and a taste for Egyptology. The former he gratified during his annual visits to his native Kintyre, and many of his researches on the life, history, and habits of the deep-sea fishes were published in the columns of the Glasgow Herald. He was also interested in the pathology of the inhabitants of the sea, and when he succeeded in capturing a diseased fish his pathological friends in Glasgow were frequently called to his aid. His taste for Egyptology was, perhaps, less known to his professional brethren, and we only became acquainted with it when, on one occasion, he delivered a popular lecture on the subject of his studies of the life and manners of ancient Egypt. The lecture betrayed an amount of research which was surprising when we remembered how busy in professional work the lecturer must have been when his researches were carried out. Altogether, Dr. Dunlop was a good all-round man, possessed of a thorough knowledge of human nature. He was a Volunteer medical officer of long standing, and formed one of the Queen's guard of honour when Her late Majesty visited Loch Katrine in 1859 to open the waterworks there. At the outbreak of the Crimean War he volunteered for active medical service, but was told he was too young. In January, 1900, he went to the Cape, and did active duty in the hospital at Wynberg. We are sure that no more enthusiastic medical Volunteer proceeded to the assistance of his countrymen in South Africa; and it is a striking circumstance that although, on account of youth, he could not help the soldiers in the Crimea, he was permitted to do a valuable work for his country when he was old and approaching the gates of death. Dr. Dunlop also gave evidence before the South African Hospital Commission. To the medical profession of Glasgow Dr. Dunlop was best known as a surgeon and as a medico-legal expert. For over twenty years he was one of the visiting surgeons to the Glasgow Royal Infirmary, his whole connection with this institution having extended to the long period of about forty years. From 1869 to 1895 he lectured on systematic surgery at Anderson's College. He was a good type of the older school of surgeons; a practical man in all his ways, and forming his judgments with shrewd commonsense. Though [Page 282] 282 Obituary. what was known as a practical man, he took a great and a critical interest in the scientific researches of the younger surgeons, and none knew good scientific work better, when he saw it, than Dr. James Dunlop. His long experience as medico-legal examiner for the City of Glasgow gave his opinion on all such matters the weight of authority. We have frequently admired in the post-mortem room the almost intuitive manner in which he unravelled the mystery of a difficult criminal case. In the witness-box his equanimity was difficult to disturb and his evidence not easy to break down. For many years Dr. Dunlop took an active interest in the affairs of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons, and some years ago he filled the office of Visitor. In his later years he acted as a Governor of the Victoria Infirmary and of the Samaritan Hospital for Women, devoting much of his time to the affairs of these institutions. Dr. Dunlop was born in Campbeltown, and was educated at the grammar school there. He took his degree of M.D. at the University of Glasgow in 1857, and was admitted a Fellow of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons on 4th June, 1860. His whole professional life was passed in Glasgow. His wife and six sons and two daughters survive him. Of his sons, one, Dr. Binnie Dunlop, is at present on active service as a civil surgeon in South Africa, and another is a member of the English Bar. Dr. Dunlop was too busy a man for many contributions to medical literature; but the following list of papers from his pen will show the bent of his mind in professional writing:—(1) "Notes on Acupressure as applied to 'Street Surgery'" (8vo, Glasgow, 1867); (2) "Contribution to Aseptic Surgery, being Notes of Cases" (8vo, Glasgow, 1876); (3) "Notes on Post-mortem Examinations in Criminal Cases conducted by the Crown Officials in Glasgow" (8vo, 1893); (4) "Address to the Glasgow Southern Medical Society on the Victoria Infirmary" (Glasgow, 1896); (5) "Medical Report on the Clyde Volunteer Brigade Camp at Gailes, Irvine" (1889). Douglas, 53, who worked for firms in Pawtucket during the past 15 years, died Thursday in St. Joseph's Hospital, Providence, after a brief illness. He resided at 644 River avenue, Providence. He was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, a son of the late Robert and Elizabeth (Anderson) Douglas. He had been employed by Bond Clothing Co. and later was in business for himself as a window display man. Besides his widow, Constance (Darcy) Douglas, he leaves three daughters, Sister Mary Laurene, O.P., of St. Dominic's Convent, Blauvelt, N. Y., Mrs. Constance Garceau of Warwick and Miss Norma Douglas of Providence, and a sister, Mrs. Thomas Crombie of Chicago. A funeral service will be held at 10 a. m., Monday from the Ruth E. This is an analysis, not a finding of fact, and accuses no one of a crime. Sir Nathaniel Dunlop has the stronger documented connection to the estate gatherings of 1906. His nephew Binnie was a physician, which makes him relevant to the family account. The July newspaper places Nathaniel at Shieldhill. No source presented here places either man with Agnes. The Case for Sir Nathaniel Dunlop brings together the records. What the records establish On June 14, 1907, at nine in the evening, Agnes Brown gave birth in Edinburgh. She signed the registration as Lawrence Brown’s mother, recorded her occupation as domestic servant and gave Gean Cottage, Shieldhill as her usual home. The father’s entry is blank. Laurence’s daughter described “a doctor at the estate”. She did not identify a Dunlop by name. Nathaniel acquired an honorary doctorate after the estimated conception. Binnie already held a medical qualification. Who first used the description, and when, matters to its interpretation. The 1861 household and Dr James Dunlop’s 1901 obituary establish the kinship. Binnie’s 1907 medical register gives a Glasgow address. His former school’s register in 1905 gives an Essex address. Neither is a record of attendance at Shieldhill. “The Archibald connection goes back to Agnes’s childhood. In 1891, five-year-old Agnes appears in household schedule 7. Mary and Alexander Archibald appear in schedule 5, with one household enumerated between them. In 1901, Mary was a sewing mistress at Gean Tree Cottages, and Agnes lived with her uncle at Lime Tree Cottage. That same year Alexander was recorded at Shieldhill as a domestic gardener, heading a household with his wife Annie and a servant, Susan Cumisky. These entries give us a sound reason to investigate whether Mary helped Agnes. They leave open who occupied Agnes’s particular cottage in 1907, who attended her pregnancy, and where on the estate Alexander slept. 1891 households · 1901 cottage households · Alexander’s household “Then there is Edinburgh. On April 2, 1911, three-year-old Laurence B. Douglas was listed as ‘Son’ in the Douglas household at 16 Lochrin Place. Your point about the distance holds up. The former maternity hospital at 79 Lauriston Place stands about one-fifth of a mile straight-line from the centre of the modern postcode covering No. 16. That is a postcode estimate rather than a door-to-door measurement. The uncertainty that matters more is when. Nearly four years separate the birth and the census. We know where Laurence was born and where he was living by age three. We still need the first dated record that puts him in Lizzie’s care.” 1911 census page portal.historicenvironment.scot The question I’d press hardest Did Agnes go to Edinburgh because someone had already arranged for Lizzie to take the baby? That is a sharper question than why Agnes passed up Glasgow. Edinburgh’s Royal Maternity Hospital regularly admitted unmarried women. On the very page where Agnes registered Laurence, the next entry records another unmarried domestic servant who delivered at the same hospital six days later. Agnes had a reason to seek care there independent of either family. What would distinguish her case is a record placing Lizzie, Mary, a Dunlop, or another named intermediary in the arrangements for Agnes or the baby. Birth-register page, entries 839–840 pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov For paternity, the priorities are a contemporary acknowledgment or support record and dated evidence of contact with Agnes. For placement, the hospital register and evidence about the Douglas household may explain how Laurence reached Lizzie. These questions could have different answers. The evidence places Sir Nathaniel at a 1906 estate gathering and identifies Binnie as his physician nephew. It warrants pursuing Sir Nathaniel first. The Edinburgh evidence can help trace the child’s care. It has yet to identify his father. New evidence: Shieldhill Hall, community activities, and possible intermediaries Source supplied for verification: Hamilton Advertiser , 6 April 1907, “An Interesting Amateur Entertainment.” The author has supplied excerpts and a summary; the complete newspaper page and its original image must be attached before this is classified as a verified full transcription. The newspaper account describes winter evening classes at the Quothquan hall, reportedly begun more than a year before publication, approximately early 1906. A governess from Glasgow taught twice weekly. Activities included music, singing and needlework for young women, with a daytime social hour for mothers and older women. The account mentions farm servants learning musical notation, a choir associated with Sunday evening services, and Ellen Dunlop playing the organ. At a concert reported as taking place the preceding Friday, approximately 29 March 1907, the audience reportedly numbered about 200. Nathaniel Dunlop chaired the gathering and Ellen Dunlop played the piano. This establishes a reported instance of the estate owner personally participating in the hall's activities during Agnes Brown's pregnancy. It does not place him at Shieldhill at the estimated conception date in autumn 1906, nor identify Agnes or Dr Binnie Dunlop among attendees. Geographic relationship Gean Tree Cottage, Shieldhill Road, Quothquan, Biggar ML12 6ND, and Shieldhill Hall, Shieldhill Road, Quothquan, Biggar ML12 6FP, are distinct identifiable properties. The existing estate research estimates their separation at approximately 400 feet (122 metres) , as a straight-line map estimate, not a surveyed or verified walking distance. Modern addresses identify the locations; a historical Ordnance Survey map should be used to verify the 1903–1907 layout. View the two properties on a map . What the evidence does and does not establish Documented in the reported article: repeated instruction and community gatherings; women and servants participated as groups; Nathaniel and Ellen were personally involved in the March 1907 concert. Opportunity, not attendance: Agnes was a young domestic servant who gave Gean Cottage as her home in July 1907. Her proximity and demographic fit make participation possible, but the article does not name her, Mary Archibald, Alexander Archibald, the Douglases, or Binnie Dunlop. Not a documented singles event: the article describes education, music, choir and social activities, not organized matchmaking. Construction hypothesis: Nathaniel and Ellen financed the hall in 1903. Nathaniel may have visited during construction, but no dated building-site attendance, contractor account, or supervision record has been identified. Financing does not prove how often he visited. Placement hypothesis: a potential chain through Ellen, the Archibald family, church or hospital contacts is worth testing. No record presently shows who financed Agnes's cottage, travel, care or Laurence's placement. 1929 travel: Laurence's passage occurred 22 years later, after Nathaniel's death. Existing ship and border documentation reportedly identifies self-payment; the original fare fields should be retained as exhibits rather than presenting an estate-funded passage as fact. Next records: original newspaper page and follow-up Quothquan columns; hall attendance and concert programs; the Glasgow governess's identity; 1903 construction accounts; estate tenancy and payroll; maternity hospital records LHB3/14/6 and LHB3/16/3.
