x: Cold Case File · Case analysis Case presentation: who fathered Laurence? Written by Claude (Anthropic), November 22, 2026, at Doug Garceau's request. Question put: "If you were a police detective or prosecutor, how would you present this case to a grand jury?" This is an analysis of the exhibits in this file. It is not a finding of fact and accuses no one of a crime. Opening statement On the evidence of his documented appearances, Sir Nathaniel is the first of the two Dunlop men to investigate. His nephew Binnie supplies a second line through his medical qualification. The birth entry names neither man. The Case for Sir Nathaniel Dunlop reviews each dated sighting and the competing interpretations. Part 1. The family that owned the place where Agnes lived Sir Nathaniel Dunlop owned Shieldhill, a large country house in Lanarkshire, from 1898. He was knighted in July 1907, one month after Laurence was born. 1861 census, 50 Abbotsford Place, Glasgow: Archibald Dunlop's household includes sons Nathaniel, 31, and James, 27, physician and surgeon. James was the knight's brother. Binnie Dunlop was born 3 August 1874 to Dr James Dunlop and Jane Menzies Binnie. James's obituary (Glasgow Medical Journal, April 1901) names "Dr. Binnie Dunlop" as his son. Binnie was the knight's nephew. That relationship is proven. The medical register gave Binnie’s professional address as 16 Carlton Place, Glasgow, through 1907 and Woodford Green from 1908. His former school already listed the Essex address in 1905. These entries cannot date a move or locate him on a particular day. Part 2. The gardener and his sister 1901 census: Alexander Archibald, 30, domestic gardener at Shieldhill, living there with his wife Annie and a servant. He worked for the Dunlops. Where the gardener lived (added after review): the 1901 census lists Alexander's household at the address "Shieldhill" itself (Libberton ED 3, schedule 3), not at a lodge or cottage, and the household kept its own live-in servant, Susan Cumisky, 26, which is unusual for a gardener. On census night Sir Nathaniel was in Glasgow, at 1 Montgomerie Crescent, Partick, with his daughter Ellen and seven servants. So in 1901 the gardener's family was the household recorded at Shieldhill while the owner was away, which suggests they may have been living in, or keeping, the house. The census does not say which building they occupied, and no record yet shows the gardener and the knight under the same roof. If they were in the house, the gardener's family would have been the people who knew who came and went at Shieldhill. Mary Archibald, born 23 October 1864, Alexander's sister, was at Gean Tree Cottages in 1901. Agnes Brown as a neighbor: in 1891 Agnes, age 5, was listed one household from Alexander and Mary. In 1901 she was at Lime Tree Cottage, close to Mary. The Archibalds had known her since she was a small child. The two cottage entries. The 1901 census placed Mary Archibald at Gean Tree Cottages and Agnes at Lime Tree Cottage. Agnes gave Gean Cottage as her own address in 1907. A rental or dated household record is needed to establish whether Mary was still there and whether they lived together. Laurence's 1907 birth entry: Agnes, domestic servant, gives her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, and signs as the mother. No father is named. Part 2b. The hall at the heart of the village (added after review) Distances, measured from map coordinates: Gean Tree Cottage, the home Agnes gave on the birth entry, is about 400 feet in a straight line from Shieldhill Hall, the corrugated-iron hall Nathaniel and Ellen Dunlop put up in 1903 (listed building LB12995, grid reference NS 99544 39695). Shieldhill House, the Dunlops' own house, is about 0.9 mile from the cottage. The hall was the centre of village life, and the Dunlops were in it in person. The Hamilton Advertiser reported, on December 30, 1905, a lecture given "through the invitation of Mr and Miss Dunlop" and a Christmas party in Shieldhill Hall, "generously entertained by Mr and Miss Dunlop." On April 6, 1907 it reported that "the lady of the manor," Ellen, had for more than a year run winter evening classes in the hall: a lady governess came from Glasgow two days a week to teach the women of the village, the young people learned music and singing, Ellen played the organ, and "some of the farm servants excel in the reading of the notes." At the closing concert, about March 29, 1907, some 200 people from the village and neighbourhood attended, "the laird of Shieldhill himself took the chair, and his daughter presided at the piano." These were routine, reported events, and the young servants of the estate were part of them, a few hundred yards from Agnes's door, during the months she was pregnant. The January 4, 1902 Hamilton Advertiser reported a New Year supper and dance inside the mansion for tenants, villagers and estate and house servants. Nathaniel and Ellen were present. The report describes a particular evening. It supplies neither a yearly guest list nor an entry for Agnes. A festival for working girls at Shieldhill, July 1906. On Wednesday, July 11, 1906, about two months before Agnes became pregnant, the Biggar and Culter branch of the Scotch Girls' Friendly Society held its annual festival at Shieldhill "by the kind invitation of Miss Dunlop" (Hamilton Advertiser, July 21, 1906, page 5, British Newspaper Archive; newspaper clipping ). The Girls' Friendly Society was a church society for young working women, many of them domestic servants ("members"), overseen by ladies ("associates"). More than seventy came by carriage from Biggar. Ellen met them at Quothquan and took them to the hall for a short service, and then they all went on to the mansion for tea, walks in the gardens, and boating on the pond. "Mr Dunlop, on his arrival from the city, gave a cordial welcome to all." The report gives no list of names, so it does not show whether Agnes was there. It does show the Dunlops hosting young working women at the house itself, with Nathaniel present, in the summer of 1906. The village social of March 1906. On Friday, March 9, 1906, the Quothquan Bowling Club held its annual social in the village schoolroom (Hamilton Advertiser, March 17, 1906, page 6, British Newspaper Archive). The paper says nearly every family in the Quothquan district was there, with guests from Libberton, Thankerton and Biggar, and about seventy sat down to supper. Mr Scott of Eastertown spoke first, and the Rev. Mr Picken of Shieldhill Hall proposed a toast to two members, Mr James Wilson and Mr Walter Frood, who were leaving to start business in Montana. A dance followed, with the music by Mr and Miss Jackson ( newspaper clipping ). A Mr Jackson was also one of the singers at the 1902 New Year dance in the mansion. The report names no Dunlop, and no one named in it is Agnes. It shows how often the whole village, servants included, gathered together in the year Agnes became pregnant. The classes were still running in 1910, with a singer from Glasgow. On Tuesday, March 29, 1910, the annual entertainment for the winter evening classes was held in the Quothquan Hall before a crowded audience from the village and neighbourhood, with Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill presiding (Hamilton Advertiser, April 2, 1910, page 6, British Newspaper Archive; newspaper clipping ). Mr W. F. Addie of Biggar taught violin. Miss Reid led a choir, and "Miss Reid, of Glasgow" sang several pieces. Miss Dunlop was praised for the great interest she took in the welfare of the locality. Mrs M'Lellan ran the needlework class, the Rev. M. Picken gave an address, and the performers were given supper afterwards. The 1907 report described a governess coming from Glasgow two days a week to teach the classes. Miss Reid of Glasgow may be that teacher, which still needs checking. The records connect Agnes to a cottage address and a birth in Edinburgh. The questions are who, if anyone, helped her during the pregnancy and how Laurence came into the Douglas household. Neither the gardener nor an estate payment has been established in that chain. Part 3. The choice of hospital Most women gave birth at home. National Records of Scotland estimates that about 95% of all births in this period, among rich and poor alike, were home births (National Records of Scotland, "Safe delivery: a history of Scottish midwives"). Agnes had a home: on the birth entry she gave her domicile as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, the estate owned by the knight, Binnie Dunlop's uncle. She could have given birth there with a local midwife, as most women did. Instead she went about 25 miles to a hospital in another city. That makes the hospital birth itself unusual, before even asking why it was Edinburgh. Agnes’s recorded destination was Edinburgh. Home delivery, medical advice and personal contacts are among the possibilities to consider. No letter, referral or diary records which choices Agnes considered. The journey itself (added after review). Going to Edinburgh meant a train trip of roughly 25 miles from the Biggar area, very likely with a change of trains, late in pregnancy. That is a hard and risky journey for a woman close to giving birth, made when a home birth with a local midwife was the normal choice. When Agnes travelled is not yet known. Unmarried women were often admitted to the Edinburgh hospital before labour, for shelter, so she may have gone days or weeks ahead. Either way, the trip took planning. From the Biggar area the line most likely ran on the Caledonian Railway into Edinburgh's Princes Street station, about two-thirds of a mile from the hospital, partly uphill by Lothian Road and Lauriston. Her train time and travel date are not recorded, so the weather on her journey cannot be known. The hospital casebook for June 1907 should give her admission date, which would show how far ahead the trip was arranged. Three years and ten months later, the baby is living about half a mile from that hospital. Laurence was born on June 14, 1907, at the Royal Maternity Hospital in Edinburgh. The next civil entry records another unmarried domestic servant who gave birth there. Agnes’s own admission and discharge entries may help explain her circumstances. Her choice of city identifies neither a financier nor a father. Part 4. Where the baby went 1911 census, 16 Lochrin Place, Edinburgh: Elizabeth (Lizzie) Douglas, her daughter Janet, and three-year-old "Laurence B.," recorded as son. Lochrin Place is about 0.2 miles from the maternity hospital. The gap (added after review): Laurence's whereabouts between his birth in Edinburgh on 14 June 1907 and the census of 2 April 1911 are unknown. No record shows him going back to Shieldhill. What is known is that Agnes was still in Edinburgh on 4 July 1907, twenty days after the birth, when she registered him at St Giles. The weather (Leith observations, found by ChatGPT): on 14 June 1907, the day of the birth at 9 p.m., it was 52°F with three-quarters cloud at 8 a.m. and 59°F and overcast at 6 p.m. On 4 July, the day she registered him, it was 50°F and overcast at 8 a.m. and 49°F with rain at 6 p.m. The registration hour is not recorded. The St Giles registrar was at 24 Forrest Road in the 1907 directories (found by ChatGPT): about 0.41 miles in a straight line from the hospital, and about 0.58 miles from 18 Lochrin Place, both an easy walk. She gave Gean Cottage as her home, but that is the address she claimed, not proof she went back there, or that the baby did. No legal adoption existed (added after review): legal adoption did not exist in Scotland until the Adoption of Children (Scotland) Act 1930. Before that, a child could only be handed to another family informally: nothing was filed and the birth entry never changed. That fits the records. Agnes registered him on 4 July 1907 under her own surname, as Lawrence Brown. At home he was Laurence B. Douglas, listed as Lizzie's son in 1911. When he emigrated in 1929 he travelled as Lawrence Brown, because his birth entry was still his only legal identity. The "B." in "Laurence B. Douglas" most likely kept that Brown, his mother's name, inside the name he used every day. The Brown name stayed with him all his life. The likeliest reading is that Agnes handed him to the Douglases directly. Lizzie's own history: born 31 May 1874 at Gilmerton to Ann McDonald, domestic servant. The entry is marked illegitimate and names no father. She was raised by her grandparents and put their names in the parents' column when she married Robert Douglas in 1899. She had lived the same path Laurence did. The neighborhood: every address for Lizzie is within a mile of the hospital: 4 Hatton Place (1899), 5 Beaumont Place (1901), 16 Lochrin Place (1911). Agnes stayed near her son: Agnes did not go back to the estate for good. By 1911 she was a nurse at the Royal Edinburgh Asylum in Morningside. She married Thomas McKay McKenzie there on 28 August 1911, before the same registrar who had recorded Laurence's birth. In 1912 she was at 9 Stewart Terrace, and in 1915 at 62 Balcarres Street ( 1912 birth ; 1915 army papers ). Each of these three places is only about 1.1 to 1.2 miles in a straight line from 16 Lochrin Place, where Laurence was living as Laurence B. Douglas in 1911. Gean Tree Cottage is about 25 miles away. (The Douglases moved to Dunfermline in 1912, so from then on Laurence was farther away.) Part 5. The witness Ever since Doug was young, his mother, Laurence's daughter, has said without hesitation that the father was a doctor at the estate, and that a gardener took him in. She said it for decades, long before any of these records were found. The records identify a gardener and two distinct uses of “doctor”. They leave the identities and actions described by the family account open. The doctor. There was a doctor in the estate owner's own family: Dr Binnie Dunlop, nephew of Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill. The gardener. Alexander Archibald’s 1901 household address reads “Shieldhill.” The entry does not specify the building he occupied. Mary Archibald, the gardener’s sister, lived at Gean Tree Cottages in 1901. Agnes gave Gean Cottage as her own address in 1907. Their proximity is worth investigating. There is no contemporary account of Mary sheltering Agnes or Alexander taking the baby. The testimony directs the search to people and records. Identifying people who fit a description still leaves their individual roles to be established. Part 6. The theory of the case A July 1906 newspaper places Nathaniel welcoming visitors to Shieldhill. Binnie was the estate owner’s nephew. A dated visit by him in 1906 remains unverified. Agnes, a young servant whose life centred on Shieldhill, became pregnant around September 1906. Did the Archibald family help Agnes during her pregnancy? The census and the birth registration suggest where to look for an answer. Agnes delivered her son in Edinburgh. Her reason for going there is unrecorded. The 1911 census places the boy with Lizzie Douglas. When and through whom he reached her household is unknown. A possibility to test: in the twenty days between the birth and the registration, Agnes may have stayed with, or visited, the Douglases near the hospital, to see that the baby was going to a safe home, before registering him on 4 July. No record yet shows Agnes there. But the Douglases can now be placed near the hospital at the time: a Robert Douglas, with an occupation matching Lizzie's husband, is listed at 18 Lochrin Place in the Edinburgh electoral rolls for both 1906–07 and 1907–08 (reported by ChatGPT; printed entries being checked). Measured from map coordinates, 18 Lochrin Place is about 0.19 miles (about 330 yards) in a straight line from the hospital door at 79 Lauriston Place, roughly a third of a mile, five to seven minutes, on foot by Lauriston Place and Tollcross. The 1879 hospital building still stands, now a hotel. That is next door to No. 16, where the 1911 census found Laurence, and well under half a mile from the hospital. The hospital's record of where Agnes went on discharge would test the rest. Binnie had addresses associated with Glasgow and Essex. Their dates do not establish when he travelled between them. Part 6b. The case for Sir Nathaniel himself (added November 22, 2026) Newspaper research since this presentation was first written makes Sir Nathaniel Dunlop, not his nephew, the stronger candidate on the documents. He was there. The papers place him at Shieldhill among his servants and villagers: the New Year supper and dance in the mansion house for "tenantry, villagers, estate and house servants" (1902); the Girls' Friendly Society festival for young working women at Shieldhill on July 11, 1906, where "Mr Dunlop, on his arrival from the city, gave a cordial welcome to all," about two months before Agnes became pregnant; and the hall concert he chaired in 1907. No record yet places Binnie at Shieldhill at all. The 1906 water-supply report establishes Nathaniel’s ownership of houses at Quothquan. It does not identify the proprietor or tenant of Gean Cottage by name. His honorary law degree dates to April 1907, after the estimated conception. Newspapers later styled him “Dr”. Binnie held a medical qualification. The family recollection leaves both interpretations open. His positions in shipping and the Clyde Trust attest to his means. No account, receipt or letter identifies a payment on Agnes’s behalf. Against him: he was about 76 in the autumn of 1906 (he was 31 in the 1861 census). The papers place him in Glasgow on June 21 and July 2, 1907, and nowhere yet in Edinburgh during Agnes's stay there. Part 7. What the defense would say No record puts Binnie at Shieldhill or near Agnes. This is the biggest gap. Estate gardeners lived on the estate. That was his job. The census gives the address as Shieldhill, not which building. Agnes was the Archibalds' neighbor for 16 years. That Mary supervised the pregnancy is a reasonable guess, but no record says it. Other men were at Shieldhill: the knight, staff, visitors, men in the village. The records name none of them either way. The birth register itself shows Agnes was not unusual at that hospital: the very next entry, six days later, is another unmarried domestic servant who also delivered there. Unmarried servants going to the Edinburgh hospital was a known path. Edinburgh has innocent explanations: a large teaching hospital that took unmarried women, distance from Agnes's own community, or a referral by a church, employer or midwife. Doctors moved to England for jobs and marriages. The family account is secondhand and over a century old. "A doctor" could describe many men. The "B" in "Laurence B." most likely stands for Brown, his mother's surname, not Binnie. No record yet shows how Agnes's side connected to Lizzie's side. Part 8. Assessment Sir Nathaniel is the stronger of the two estate leads because of the contemporary record of his presence. Binnie has the closer occupational fit. Neither man has a documented meeting with Agnes, and Laurence’s father remains unidentified. Part 9. Records that could settle it DNA: an autosomal test from Laurence's daughter, his closest living relative, compared against descendants of the Dunlop and Binnie families. Royal Maternity Hospital register, June 1907 (Lothian Health Services Archive): referral, prior address, and who received the baby. The hospital Register of Births (LHSA, LHB3/14): it can record where each mother went after the birth. Agnes's line could show where she, and perhaps the baby, went next. Barbara Shirra, entry 840: another unmarried domestic servant, who delivered six days after Agnes and registered her daughter on the same day (4 July 1907, consecutive entries 839 and 840). Barbara was Edinburgh-born and in 1901 was a pupil at Dr Guthrie's Original Industrial School for Girls, which trained girls for domestic service and placed them in jobs. The school's registers (National Records of Scotland, GD425) could show where it placed her, and whether that was near Agnes or Lizzie. This is a lead into the servant network, not evidence of one. A paternity decree: a sheriff-court action for support may appear as a Register of Corrected Entries note on Laurence's birth entry. Poor law records: parish relief files often named the alleged father. Kirk session minutes, Libberton and Quothquan: churches often recorded the man's name. Shieldhill estate papers and the local press, 1906: guests, family visits, Binnie's movements. Binnie's letters to Marie Stopes, 1916–1945, British Library Add MS 58564. Conclusion: the evidence justifies a full investigation. It does not yet justify a conclusion. ← Back to the Cold Case File ChatGPT's presentation →

t: Duchess of Bedford voyage of 1929 | Cold Case File
x: Contents Findings established by the passenger records Chronology and the two Canadian port names Passenger comparison and all identified numbers The Duchess of Bedford in 1928 and 1929 Three photographs of the actual ship Cabin class comfort and life aboard Cash fares and 2026 purchasing power Luggage and the onward journey Open questions and the documents that could answer them Exhibit handling and transcription status Exhibit A British outward passenger list Exhibit B United States passenger manifest first half Exhibit C United States passenger manifest continuation Exhibit D Detroit border entry card Sources and references Laurence Brown and Janet Crombie traveled in cabin class aboard Canadian Pacific’s Duchess of Bedford, embarking at Greenock on 7 September 1929. This finding is established by their entries on the British outward passenger sheet headed Cabin. Laurence’s Detroit entry card records landing at Quebec on 13 September and U.S. admission at Detroit on 15 September. The manifest names Quebec and Montreal together, while a later card names Montreal. Those different entries are retained below. [ P1 , P2 , P3 , P4 , P5 ] The file brings together the passenger records, three actual 1928 interior photographs, contemporary ship evidence, financial calculations and a record of the remaining questions. Passenger-specific facts, descriptions of the vessel and comparisons from other dates have separate source labels. The four principal 1929 image pages and their existing Cold Case File transcriptions are reproduced in the exhibits. Findings established by the passenger records Question Finding Evidence Travel class Cabin for both Janet and Laurence; the outward sheet’s class heading applies to their rows. [ P1 ] Embarkation Greenock, Scotland, 7 September 1929. [ P1 , P2 ] Contracted landing port Montreal, through ditto marks in the outward list. [ P1 ] Laurence’s recorded landing QUEBEC, P.Q.; 9/13/29 on the contemporaneous Detroit card. [ P4 ] Manifest arrival heading QUEBEC & MONTREAL; 13 September 1929. [ P3 ] Entry into the United States Laurence: Detroit, 15 September 1929; later petition specifies C.P.R.R. [ P4 , P6 ] Money and fare payer Laurence’s card: $50; Self. Manifest: both meet the $50 threshold and both report self-paid passage. [ P3 , P4 ] Assigned cabin and actual fare Neither is identified in the inspected passenger documents. [ P1 , P2 , P3 , P4 ] Names are preserved by document. The outward list uses Laurence Brown; the U.S. manifest and Detroit card use Lawrence Brown. [ P1 , P2 , P3 ] The Duchess of Bedford in 1928 and 1929 The vessel was a new Canadian Pacific Atlantic liner built by John Brown and Company at Clydebank, yard 518. National Records of Scotland dates her launch to 24 January 1928. Her sister ships were Duchess of Atholl, Duchess of Richmond and Duchess of York. Wellington City Archives records the maiden Liverpool–Quebec–Montreal sailing as 1 June 1928, making her approximately fifteen months into service when Laurence and Janet sailed. [ S1 , S10 ] Particular Evidence-supported description Ship’s name and operator Duchess of Bedford; Canadian Pacific. Official number 160482 on the outward list. [ P1 ] Type Turbine steamship with two propellers. [ S9 , S10 ] Size About 600 feet overall. Crowe’s engineering table uses 600 feet and rounded 20,120 gross tons; the archive catalogue gives 20,123 GRT. [ S9 , S10 ] Original accommodation capacity 580 cabin, 480 tourist and 510 third class; total 1,570 passenger places. Capacity is not the number carried on this voyage. [ S10 ] Service output and speed 18,000 shaft horsepower; 17.5 knots in the builder’s engineering account. These are service particulars, not a measured average for September 1929. [ S9 ] Turbines Three turbines drive each shaft through reduction gearing: six turbines for two propellers. [ S9 ] Boilers Six main Yarrow water-tube boilers and two auxiliary cylindrical boilers; main steam 350 psi at 686°F. [ S9 ] Electrical supply Two turbo-generators totaling 1,000 kW and two diesel generators totaling 900 kW in the engineering table. [ S9 ] The machinery source is a 1948 paper by T. A. Crowe, John Brown’s engineering director, explicitly describing the original 1928 installation. It is used for that installation rather than for a later passenger refit. Gross register tonnage measures enclosed volume, not the vessel’s weight. The smaller registered-tonnage figure on the outward form is kept separate from the gross figure. [ S9 , P1 ] Later history helps identify misleading illustrations: the ship served during the Second World War, was rebuilt and renamed Empress of France after the war, and was withdrawn in 1960. Postwar accommodation capacities, altered funnels or later room arrangements do not describe the ship Laurence and Janet boarded. The 1928 photographs below avoid that date confusion. [ S4 ] Meals and music The dining photograph provides direct evidence of a dedicated cabin dining room with table service settings. A contemporary feature, Cabin Liners Set New Standard in The Chesterville Record of 5 July 1928, reports an orchestra playing in the Cabin Dining Room. It describes transmission of the music to other passenger areas by microphones and amplifiers. This establishes shipboard musical provision before the family’s voyage; it does not record the program on any September 1929 evening. [ S2 , S14 ] No menu from the 7–13 September 1929 crossing, dining-room seating list, meal-time schedule or individual account has been recovered in the inspected material. Consequently, no breakfast, lunch, dinner, afternoon tea, wine, dish or table companion is assigned to Laurence or Janet. A menu for another ship, another class or another year would be comparison evidence only. The Bodleian catalogue identifies a Duchess of Bedford farewell dinner menu dated 15 May 1930, Sayers 35 CP20, but its contents have not been inspected. [ R2 ] Services described in the same ship’s 1931 booklet This is a dated comparison: the cabin passenger booklet for 4 September 1931 describes steward wake calls, a dinner bugle thirty minutes beforehand, a purser’s safe, paid accommodation upgrades, deck games, board games, library books and shoe cleaning. It also lists infant cots, a stenographer, a surgeon and nurses, life belts, postal and wireless services, currency exchange and onward travel assistance. Deck chairs, rugs and cushions were separately rented at $1.50 each. Some services therefore carried additional charges. These rules and charges are not certified as the September 1929 terms, and the booklet does not show which services Laurence or Janet used. [ S11 ] The surviving digital material used here includes the 1931 booklet’s cover, route chart and the archive’s transcribed passenger information. It is not a complete page-by-page facsimile of that booklet. Its issue date and route must remain attached whenever its images are displayed. [ P3 , P4 , M4 ] What can be said about cabin class fares No September 1929 Duchess of Bedford cabin tariff, receipt, agent’s invoice or ticket face has been recovered. The records establish the travel class and declared payer, not the fare. The 1928 advertisement’s $200 and $300 figures concern West Indies cruises from New York lasting sixteen or twenty-nine days. They are not prices for this Atlantic crossing. [ P1 , P3 , P4 , S8 ] A contemporary comparison gives scale without supplying their fare: Marcia Clarke Davenport’s March 1929 New Yorker article reports winter cabin-liner crossings at US$150–$175 generally. Canadian Pacific’s September westbound sailing is not specifically priced. At March 1929 CPI 17.0, those amounts equal roughly US$2,978–$3,474 in October 2026 purchasing power. This is an industry benchmark, not a fare range established for either traveler. [ S13 , M1 , M2 ] If a sterling fare is later obtained, convert the original fare using a historical exchange rate before calculating its U.S. purchasing-power equivalent. The official September 1929 monthly rate was US$4.8482 per £1. Thus a verified September sterling amount would be multiplied by 4.8482 and then by 337.511/17.3. That is about US$94.59 in October 2026 purchasing power per 1929 pound; it is not a modern pound-to-dollar exchange quotation. [ M1 , M2 , M4 ] Who paid and what the records do not prove Both travelers’ manifest entries report self-paid passage; Laurence’s Detroit card repeats Self. This is evidence of their declared payment arrangements. It does not document the original source of every pound or dollar they possessed, a bank balance, savings history, a gift, a loan or a third party’s involvement. Janet’s occupation H’wife and Laurence’s Grocer are reported occupations, not income figures. Their class of travel alone cannot identify a financier. [ P1 , P2 , P3 , P4 ] The cash shown at inspection is separate from the fare already paid. Adding $50 to an unverified fare would create a speculative total travel budget. A complete cost reconstruction would require the actual ocean tickets, any rail coupons, booking date, currency, cabin grade, return-ticket terms, taxes, baggage charges and onboard expenses. None of those unknown sums is inserted into the account. The scale of the investigation An Extraordinary Family Investigation What began as an effort to understand one man's life has grown into an extensive historical investigation spanning generations, countries, institutions, and more than a century of surviving records. Researchers have assembled civil registrations, census returns, passenger manifests, medical registers, weather records, newspaper accounts, estate histories, photographs, maps, family testimony, and original archival documents. Together, these sources reveal the people and communities surrounding Laurence Brown Douglas, born Lawrence Brown in Edinburgh on June 14, 1907. The investigation reaches far beyond conventional genealogy. It examines the Scottish estate where his mother lived, the influential family who owned it, the circumstances of his birth, the household that raised him, and the journey that eventually brought him to America. The Evidence Vault opens this extraordinary collection to the public. Visitors can inspect the documents, trace the sources, examine the discoveries, and follow the questions that remain unanswered. This is not simply a family tree. It is a reconstruction of a life through the surviving historical record. And we're still discovering more. … numbered exhibits … exhibits with images … register entries tagged Newspaper … people researched Numbered exhibits and newspaper entries are included in the case register. It is owing, on the other hand, to the absence in the child-mind of both the inertia of rest and the inertia of movement that it exhibits such a high degree of suggestibility. The child-mind maintains for so short a time and in so slight a fashion any one course of action or set purpose, that almost any fresh idea—"suggestion"—from parent or playmate can turn it aside into a fresh channel, and that, in turn, can be easily supplanted by some other, newer still. There is so little mental inertia of rest belonging to the idea in possession of the mind that it can be easily supplanted, and the new idea has so little "momentum" that it can be easily turned out of its course for some new thing. Thus, a "volatile nature" is one with but slight mental functional inertia of movement; a "dogged temperament" is one with much. The great obstinacy of the uncultured, and the "fixed delusion" of the lunatic, are cases of pathologically developed psychic inertia of rest. [Double rule] Obituary. [in Gothic lettering] JAMES DUNLOP, M.D. DR. JAMES DUNLOP died, at the age of 67, at his house, 16 Carlton Place, Glasgow, on Wednesday, 13th March, 1901. By his death a well-known figure is removed from the ranks of the medical profession of Glasgow. Up till a few years ago, when failing health compelled him to give up a large portion of his work, he was one of the busiest men in the City, his public engagements being numerous and his private practice extensive. Of a genial and kindly disposition, Dr. Dunlop was much esteemed by all who came into contact with him. He was a most approachable man, who was at all times willing to do his best for those who sought his advice in cases of delicacy or difficulty. Possessed of a fund of humour and anecdote, his conversation was always interesting, and as a travelling companion he was delightful, wiling away the hours of a long journey with his vivacity and racy talk. We will not readily forget the pleasure we enjoyed in his society during a visit to Rome, when the International Medical Congress met in the Eternal City in 1894. Though even then in somewhat feeble health, his enthusiasm was great, his [Page 281] Obituary. 281 energy untiring, and his interest in the antiquities of Rome intense. All busy medical men have, or should have, a hobby or relaxation, which, on occasion, may take their minds away from the monotonous daily routine of professional work. Dr. Dunlop had two—the study of natural history, and a taste for Egyptology. The former he gratified during his annual visits to his native Kintyre, and many of his researches on the life, history, and habits of the deep-sea fishes were published in the columns of the Glasgow Herald. He was also interested in the pathology of the inhabitants of the sea, and when he succeeded in capturing a diseased fish his pathological friends in Glasgow were frequently called to his aid. His taste for Egyptology was, perhaps, less known to his professional brethren, and we only became acquainted with it when, on one occasion, he delivered a popular lecture on the subject of his studies of the life and manners of ancient Egypt. The lecture betrayed an amount of research which was surprising when we remembered how busy in professional work the lecturer must have been when his researches were carried out. Altogether, Dr. Dunlop was a good all-round man, possessed of a thorough knowledge of human nature. He was a Volunteer medical officer of long standing, and formed one of the Queen's guard of honour when Her late Majesty visited Loch Katrine in 1859 to open the waterworks there. At the outbreak of the Crimean War he volunteered for active medical service, but was told he was too young. In January, 1900, he went to the Cape, and did active duty in the hospital at Wynberg. We are sure that no more enthusiastic medical Volunteer proceeded to the assistance of his countrymen in South Africa; and it is a striking circumstance that although, on account of youth, he could not help the soldiers in the Crimea, he was permitted to do a valuable work for his country when he was old and approaching the gates of death. Dr. Dunlop also gave evidence before the South African Hospital Commission. To the medical profession of Glasgow Dr. Dunlop was best known as a surgeon and as a medico-legal expert. For over twenty years he was one of the visiting surgeons to the Glasgow Royal Infirmary, his whole connection with this institution having extended to the long period of about forty years. From 1869 to 1895 he lectured on systematic surgery at Anderson's College. He was a good type of the older school of surgeons; a practical man in all his ways, and forming his judgments with shrewd commonsense. Though [Page 282] 282 Obituary. what was known as a practical man, he took a great and a critical interest in the scientific researches of the younger surgeons, and none knew good scientific work better, when he saw it, than Dr. James Dunlop. His long experience as medico-legal examiner for the City of Glasgow gave his opinion on all such matters the weight of authority. We have frequently admired in the post-mortem room the almost intuitive manner in which he unravelled the mystery of a difficult criminal case. In the witness-box his equanimity was difficult to disturb and his evidence not easy to break down. For many years Dr. Dunlop took an active interest in the affairs of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons, and some years ago he filled the office of Visitor. In his later years he acted as a Governor of the Victoria Infirmary and of the Samaritan Hospital for Women, devoting much of his time to the affairs of these institutions. Dr. Dunlop was born in Campbeltown, and was educated at the grammar school there. He took his degree of M.D. at the University of Glasgow in 1857, and was admitted a Fellow of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons on 4th June, 1860. His whole professional life was passed in Glasgow. His wife and six sons and two daughters survive him. Of his sons, one, Dr. Binnie Dunlop, is at present on active service as a civil surgeon in South Africa, and another is a member of the English Bar. Dr. Dunlop was too busy a man for many contributions to medical literature; but the following list of papers from his pen will show the bent of his mind in professional writing:—(1) "Notes on Acupressure as applied to 'Street Surgery'" (8vo, Glasgow, 1867); (2) "Contribution to Aseptic Surgery, being Notes of Cases" (8vo, Glasgow, 1876); (3) "Notes on Post-mortem Examinations in Criminal Cases conducted by the Crown Officials in Glasgow" (8vo, 1893); (4) "Address to the Glasgow Southern Medical Society on the Victoria Infirmary" (Glasgow, 1896); (5) "Medical Report on the Clyde Volunteer Brigade Camp at Gailes, Irvine" (1889). These entries are kept separate from the numbered primary-evidence inventory to prevent double counting. Research standard: each entry distinguishes what the reported source says from what it does not establish. Add full issue, page, column, archival URL and an image or accurate transcription before promoting a lead to a verified exhibit. Nathaniel and Ellen hosted a gathering with servants among invitees. No named Agnes or Binnie; annual frequency and alcohol not established. 1903 Construction of Shieldhill Hall 1903 Historic Environment Scotland listed-building record LB12995 Shieldhill Hall described as built by Nathaniel Dunlop and Miss E. Dunlop for evening services. Joint patronage and construction attribution. No record of who supervised building or attended each day. 1905-12 Quothquan lecture and Christmas party December 1905 Local newspaper report supplied by investigation; full page outstanding Mr and Miss Dunlop reportedly hosted a lecture and Christmas entertainment. Reported Dunlop-hosted village events. Exact dates, venue, guest list, and full text require original page. 1906-03-09 Quothquan Bowling Club annual social March 9, 1906; published March 17, 1906 Hamilton Advertiser, March 17, 1906, article supplied by investigation Village schoolroom; approximately 70 at supper; Mr Scott of Eastertown presided; Rev. Picken toast; Mr and Miss Jackson supplied music. Community gathering and overlap of musicians with reported 1902 mansion event. No Agnes or Dunlop named; original page image outstanding. 1906-1907 Women's winter classes at Shieldhill Hall Operating by early 1906; reported April 6, 1907 Hamilton Advertiser, April 6, 1907, 'An Interesting Amateur Entertainment' (excerpts supplied) Twice-weekly instruction by Glasgow governess; music, singing, needlework; participation of farm servants; Ellen organist. Recurring educational and musical opportunities for women and servants. No proof Agnes attended or identification of governess; full page outstanding. 1907-03-29 Concert at Shieldhill Hall Approximately March 29, 1907; reported April 6, 1907 Hamilton Advertiser, April 6, 1907, 'An Interesting Amateur Entertainment' (excerpts supplied) Audience reportedly 200; Nathaniel chaired; Ellen played piano. Nathaniel and Ellen personally participated in a large village concert. Date inferred from 'Friday before'; no Agnes or Binnie named. 1907-06-21 Nathaniel hosts Thames Conservators in Glasgow June 21, 1907; reported June 22 The Scotsman, June 22, 1907 (research citation supplied; page outstanding) Nathaniel received Thames Conservators at Clyde Trust Buildings in Glasgow. Reported Glasgow appearance during birth-registration interval. No evidence for Edinburgh whereabouts on other dates. 1907-07-02 Clyde Trust meeting in Glasgow July 2, 1907; reported July 3 Greenock Telegraph and Belfast News-Letter, July 3, 1907 (research citations supplied) Nathaniel chaired a Clyde Trust meeting and received congratulations on knighthood. Reported Glasgow appearance. No evidence for continuous Glasgow residence. 1907-06-06 Newspaper usage of 'Dr. Nathaniel Dunlop' June 6, 1907 Naval & Military Record, June 6, 1907 (research citation supplied) Name reportedly printed as Dr. Nathaniel Dunlop. Potential contemporary use of honorary doctoral title. Full page and exact title-conferral chronology outstanding. 1907-06-22 Newspaper usage of 'Dr Nathaniel Dunlop' June 22, 1907 Daily Record (Glasgow), June 22, 1907 (research citation supplied) Speech reportedly attributes the title Dr to Nathaniel. Potential contemporary doctoral designation. Full newspaper page outstanding; not proof of medical qualification. Priority original documents 1905–1908 Lanarkshire valuation rolls, Libberton parish: Gean Tree and Lime Tree owners, occupiers and rental values. 1901 and 1911 original census images: separate cottage addresses, room counts and household identities. 1906–1907 Shieldhill estate rent books, building accounts, correspondence and guest registers, if surviving. Royal Maternity Hospital annual reports, LHB3/7, 1905–1908: Dunlop subscriptions and donations; admission registers LHB3/14/6 and LHB3/16/3. Hamilton Advertiser original pages: 1902 mansion party, December 1905 events, March 1906 Bowling Club social and April 1907 hall concert. 1911 marriage record of Agnes Brown and Thomas McKay McKenzie; Andrew and Jane Rodger marriage record; Mary Archibald's post-1901 records. Research questions: Did Agnes attend? Who employed her? Who paid for her accommodation or hospital travel? Were Nathaniel or Binnie present at Shieldhill in autumn 1906? t: Was Laurence the Son of a Knight?
x: The Names He Carried · Case LBD-001 Was Laurence the Son of a Knight? Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill Of the two Dunlop men, Sir Nathaniel has the stronger documented connection to Shieldhill in 1906. A July newspaper places him there welcoming visitors. Binnie was a medical doctor, as remembered in the family account, but his whereabouts that autumn remain open. The birth registration names neither man. The case for Sir Nathaniel Read the dated sightings, the original newspaper clipping, the role of Ellen Dunlop, and a comparison of uncle and nephew. The full discussion also considers what evidence would change the finding. Read The Case for Sir Nathaniel Dunlop The Doctor and the Gardener Laurence’s daughter has told her son the same story since he was young. She said without hesitation that Laurence’s father was a doctor at the Shieldhill estate and that a gardener took Laurence in. The doctor. The owner of Shieldhill, Sir Nathaniel Dunlop, was made an honorary Doctor of Laws in April 1907, two months before Laurence was born, and the newspapers began calling him "Dr. Nathaniel Dunlop." He also had a nephew who was a medical doctor, Binnie Dunlop. Sir Nathaniel is the stronger estate lead on the dated evidence. Laurence’s birth entry leaves the father’s name blank. We still do not know who his father was. The gardener and the main house. Alexander Archibald was a gardener. In 1901 the census gave his address as “Shieldhill”. It lists his wife Annie and a servant, Susan Cumisky, in his household. He may have lived in the main house. The entry uses only the name “Shieldhill”. Where Agnes and Laurence appear in the records. Alexander’s sister Mary lived at Gean Tree Cottages in 1901. When Agnes Brown registered Laurence’s birth in 1907, she gave her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill. By 1911, three-year-old Laurence was living with Lizzie Douglas. We still do not know who first took the baby in or who introduced Agnes to Lizzie. t: Janet's Ships
x: The Names He Carried Janet's Ships Janet Crombie (born Janet Page Douglas) · 1926, 1929, 1929. Every line is from a document or a listed source. Nothing is filled in. Janet Page Douglas, later Janet Crombie. Three crossings are on record. The ship for the first one is not known. 1. 1926: to America Date What the record says Document 16 July 1926 Janet Douglas marries Thomas Crombie, Dunfermline. Naturalization petitions of Janet Crombie (no. 329111) and Thomas Crombie (no. 327632), Chicago, as read in the book's source notes [5] . The Scottish marriage register has not been examined. Images not yet in the Cold Case File. 13 Sept 1926 Entry into the U.S. at Detroit, "C.P.R.R.," "C.P. No. 19." Same two petitions [5] . — Ship and sailing date: not recorded in any document held. 2. 1926–1929: Chicago "1926–1929 Chicago" — her answer to "Whether ever before in the United States," and "Home:-1534, South Kostner Ave., Chicago, Ills." ( List D, right, line 3 ) U.S. immigration visa no. 469891, issued at Washington, 13-4-29 ( List D, left, line 3 ). 3. May 1929: the Montroyal, Quebec to Greenock Date What the record says Document 18 May 1929 UK incoming passenger list, Montroyal from Quebec, arriving Greenock: Janet Crombie, 29, married, housewife, third class; UK address 39 Grieve Street, Dunfermline. As read in the book's source notes from the original image [5] . Image not yet in the Cold Case File. The Montroyal Earlier name Empress of Britain (1906–1923); renamed Montroyal in 1924 [1] Builder Fairfield Shipbuilding & Engineering Co., Govan; yard no. 442 [1] [4] Launched / maiden voyage 11 November 1905; maiden voyage Liverpool–Quebec, 5 May 1906 [4] Size 14,189 gross as built; 15,646 gross after the 1924 refit; 548.8 ft × 65.7 ft [2] Passengers after 1924 600 cabin class and 800 third class [2] End Her final voyage began at Antwerp on 7 September 1929 — the same day the Duchess of Bedford left Greenock with Janet and Laurence — after 190 round trips [1] . Laid up September 1929 [2] ; sold 17 June 1930 to the Stavanger Shipbreaking Co., Norway [1] . Her lounge was bought for the Sola Strand Hotel and became the Montroyal Ballroom [4] . 4. September 1929: the Duchess of Bedford, with Laurence Date What the record says Document 7 Sept 1929 Line 8: CROMBIE, Janet, 39 Greive St., Dunfermline, H'wife, 29. Ticket ...480 (32480 in the book's source notes). Her "1" is entered in the "Foreign Countries" column for country of last permanent residence. Intended residence: U.S.A. UK outward list 7 Sept 1929 Line 3: CROMBIE, Janet, 29, F, married, H'wife, British, Scots, born Edinburgh; visa 469891, Washington, 13-4-29; last permanent residence U.S.A., Chicago. List D, left 13 Sept 1929 Line 3: "Mother:-Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson, 39, Grieve St., Dunfermline." Ills., Chicago. "Home:-1534, South Kostner Ave., Chicago, Ills." Height 5 ft 0 in; complexion Fr.; hair Br.; eyes Gr. (faint copy). Her money entry cannot be read on this copy. List D, right — No Detroit border card for Janet in September 1929 is in the file. Still unknown The ship and date of her 1926 crossing. Why her 1929 visa was issued in Washington. Her 1929 border crossing card, if one was made. Images of the Montroyal list and of the two Chicago naturalization petitions, for the Cold Case File. Sources Wikipedia, RMS Empress of Britain (1905), later Montroyal Norway Heritage, S/S Montroyal GG Archives, SS Montroyal Maritimequest, Empress of Britain (1906) data The Names He Carried, source notes to Chapters 18–21 (readings from original images held by the author)

Ellen Smith (d. 1867); one child, Ellen Smith Dunlop 1867–1958, unmarried Albert Blake Darcy (1888–1957) & Eugenie Emma Delaire Married 16 Jan 1912 Child Constance Eugenie Darcy (b. 12 Oct 1912, Providence) Timeline Date Event June 14, 1907 Born Lawrence Brown at the Royal Maternity Hospital, Lauriston Place, Edinburgh. June 28, 1907 The King's birthday honours name Nathaniel Dunlop, owner of Shieldhill, for a knighthood. July 4, 1907 Birth registered by his mother, Agnes Brown, at 24 Forrest Road. July 15, 1907 Dunlop knighted at Buckingham Palace; the Gazette of July 26 gives his address as Shieldhill, Biggar. April 2, 1911 Census: Laurence B. Douglas, 3, "son," at 16 Lochrin Place, Edinburgh, with Elizabeth Douglas and her daughter Janet. August 19, 1912 Admitted to Queen Anne Infant School, Dunfermline, Fife, as Lawrence Douglas; the register calls him "Adopted" and names his guardian. January 11, 1916 Transfers to Queen Anne Primary, entry 1191; the register gives his guardian, Robert Douglas, at 5 Foundry Street, Dunfermline. April 2–3, 1916 Zeppelin raid on Leith and Edinburgh; a bomb falls on Lauriston Place, the same street as his birthplace. September 9, 1919 Robert Douglas, who raised him, dies of tuberculosis at Woodburn Sanatorium, Edinburgh, aged 43. October 8, 1920 Leaves school at thirteen, "Granted Exemption by E.A." June 19, 1921 Census: Lawrence Douglas, 14, message boy for a grocer, at 5 Foundry Street, Dunfermline; Elizabeth Douglas a widow. July 16, 1926 His sister Janet marries Thomas Crombie; she enters the U.S. at Detroit, September 13, 1926. September 7, 1929 Sails from Greenock on the Duchess of Bedford with Janet. September 13, 1929 Arrives at Quebec on the Duchess of Bedford. September 15, 1929 Enters the United States at Detroit as Lawrence Brown, age 22. October 2, 1934 Elizabeth Douglas, now Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson, enters the United States at Port Huron, Michigan, to live with Janet in Chicago. 1937–1938 Providence directories list a Lawrence Douglas, display manager, 165 Weybosset Street. September 21, 1938 The Great Hurricane floods downtown Providence. October 9, 1939 Marries Constance Eugenie Darcy in Birmingham, Alabama. 1940–1941 Window trimmer and displayman for Bond Stores, San Francisco. February 11, 1943 Petitions for naturalization in Pittsburgh as Laurence Brown Douglas. May 6, 1943 Takes the oath and is admitted a citizen of the United States, Pittsburgh. 1947 Window dresser, 97 Magill Street, Pawtucket. 1950–1955 Display worker, 148 General Street, Providence. 1956–1961 Display work, 644 River Avenue, Providence; displayman at Carter's Men Store, Pawtucket, in 1960. March 9, 1961 Dies at St. Joseph's Hospital, Providence, age 53. March 13, 1961 Funeral announced from the Ruth E. Urquhart funeral home, Warwick; burial at Saint Ann Cemetery, Cranston. December 29, 1900 Newspaper Miss Dunlop's gift for the Quothquan Christmas party Hamilton Advertiser, December 29, 1900 (British Newspaper Archive) Ellen Dunlop was providing for village events in Quothquan by 1900. New Year's evening 1902 (published January 4, 1902) Newspaper New Year supper and dance in Shieldhill House Hamilton Advertiser, January 4, 1902, page 6 (British Newspaper Archive) Mr and Miss Dunlop, "with their usual generosity," entertained the tenantry, villagers, estate and house servants to a supper and dance in the mansion house. Singers included Messrs Wilson, Henderson and Jackson. 1903 Official record Shieldhill Hall, Quothquan (listed building LB12995) Historic Environment Scotland, listed building record LB12995 The corrugated-iron hall in Quothquan was built in 1903 by Nathaniel Dunlop and Miss E. Dunlop for evening services. The listing gives its map position, used for the distance measurements below. December 1905 (published December 30, 1905) Newspaper Lecture and Christmas party in Shieldhill Hall Hamilton Advertiser, December 30, 1905, page 6 (British Newspaper Archive) A lecture given "through the invitation of Mr and Miss Dunlop," and a Christmas party in Shieldhill Hall, with the Rev. Mr and Mrs Picken present. March 9, 1906 (published March 17, 1906) Newspaper Quothquan Bowling Club annual social Hamilton Advertiser, March 17, 1906, page 6 (British Newspaper Archive) Nearly every family in the Quothquan district came to the social in the schoolroom; about seventy at supper; a dance followed, with music by Mr and Miss Jackson. No Dunlop is named. May 4, 1906 Newspaper Water supply for Mr Dunlop's houses at Quothquan Motherwell Times, May 4, 1906 (British Newspaper Archive) Nathaniel Dunlop applied for a water supply for houses at Quothquan "belonging to him": the Dunlops owned cottages in the village in 1906. July 11, 1906 (published July 21, 1906) Newspaper Girls' Friendly Society festival at Shieldhill Hamilton Advertiser, July 21, 1906, page 5 (British Newspaper Archive) By Miss Dunlop's invitation, more than seventy members and associates of the Scotch Girls' Friendly Society (a church society for young working women) had a service in the hall, then tea, garden walks and boating at Shieldhill. "Mr Dunlop, on his arrival from the city, gave a cordial welcome to all." No list of names is given. December 29, 1906 and January 12, 1907 Newspaper A new teacher appointed to Quothquan Oban Times, December 29, 1906 and January 12, 1907 (British Newspaper Archive) Miss MacLachlan, teacher at Achnacarry, left for an appointment at Quothquan in the winter Agnes was pregnant. At the closing concert the laird of Shieldhill was in the chair and Miss Dunlop played; about 200 attended. October 24, 1907 Newspaper "Dr. Nathaniel Dunlop," chairman of the Clyde Trust Liverpool Journal of Commerce, October 24, 1907 (British Newspaper Archive) Another use of the title "Dr." for Nathaniel after his April 1907 degree. x: The Names He Carried Laurence's Ship and Journey, 1929 TSS Duchess of Bedford · Canadian Pacific Steamships · September 7–15, 1929 · Laurence Brown and Janet Crombie. Every line below is from a document in the Cold Case File or from a source listed at the bottom. Nothing is filled in. TSS Duchess of Bedford. Photograph supplied by Doug Garceau; original source and date not recorded. 1. The journey, from the documents Date What the record says Document 13 Apr 1929 Janet Crombie's visa no. 469891, issued at Washington. List D, left 3 Sept 1929 U.S. immigration visa no. 27768 issued to Lawrence Brown at Glasgow, under "Sec 5" of the Act of 1924. (On the U.S. manifest the date 3.9.29 is written over another date that is struck through.) Detroit card ; List D, left 7 Sept 1929 Duchess of Bedford, official no. 160482, Canadian Pacific, sails from Greenock, bound for Quebec & Montreal. Line 8: CROMBIE, Janet, 29, H'wife. Line 9: BROWN, Laurence, 22, Grocer. Both: 39 Greive St., Dunfermline. Class column headed "Cabin." Port contracted to land: Montreal. Ticket numbers, as read in the book's source notes from the full image (image 30 of 90): Janet 32480, Laurence 33082. On the smaller copy in the file the first digits are cut off ("...480", "...082"). A pencil mark beside Laurence's line reads "USA." UK outward list 7 Sept 1929 Master's name on the outward list: two readings. The book's source notes, made from the full original image, read "H. Sibbons." Our reading of the smaller copy in the file is "R. GIBSON[?]" (uncertain). Provisions certified for 900 statute adults for a voyage of 21 days. Ship's figures written on the form: 16610 and 505. UK outward list 7 Sept 1929 U.S. alien manifest List D: Janet on line 3, Lawrence on line 10. Line 9 (Peter Ross Stewart) is struck through, "To Canada." Lines 14–31 stamped NOT USED. List D, left 13 Sept 1929 Arrival heading: "Arriving at Port of QUEBEC & MONTREAL," dated 13 SEP 1929 (date stamp faint). Lawrence's nearest relative: "Mother:- Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson, 39, Grieve St. Dunfermline." Going to: "B.-in-Law:- Mr. Thomas Crombie, 1534, So. Kostner Ave., Chicago, Ill." Passage paid by: Self. List D, right 13 Sept 1929 "Seaport of landing: QUEBEC, P.Q." Date of landing 9/13/29. Detroit card 13 Sept 1929 Back of the Detroit card: round stamp "PUBLIC HEALTH SERVICE · U.S. · PASSED · MEDICAL EXAMINATION," Quebec. Remarks: examined at Quebec, Canada, 9/13/29, signed by a U.S. Immigrant Inspector (name read as "Alfred [?] Heald [?]") and a second Immigrant Inspector ("Henry [?] Reppy [?]"). "Class: Q" written large in ink. "90-day" printed beside "514 Visitor." Two dark smudges on the card; no fingerprint can be made out on this copy. Detroit card, back 15 Sept 1929 Admitted at Detroit (stamped SEP 15 1929). Money shown $50. Purpose "Seek Work," "Perm." Previous disposition "CP #21." Present disposition "adm." Detroit card 15 Sept 1929 His own later account: entry at Detroit "under the name of Lawrence Brown on Sept. 15, 1929 on the C. P. R. R." Certificate of Arrival no. 3-234422. 1943 petition ; 1943 affidavit 21 June 1941 Later card: "MONTREAL: Sept, 1929: D/Bedford." Blaine card Weather, as recorded These readings are from the book's source notes, which cite the official weather records named; they have not been re-checked here. 7–8 Sept 1929, Scotland: Met Office Daily Weather Report — high pressure over the British Isles; forecast for southwest Scotland "Light or moderate westerly breeze; fair; warm"; Renfrew maximum 67°F, no rain. The Minnedosa reported fog west of Ireland. 8 Sept: a low near Iceland. 13 Sept 1929, Quebec: maximum 61°F, 0.43 in. of rain. Montreal (McGill): maximum 64°F, 0.64 in. of rain. (Environment and Climate Change Canada.) 15 Sept 1929, Wayne, Michigan: maximum 72°F, minimum 34°F, no rain. (NOAA GHCN-Daily.) 2. Where the records disagree Landing port: Quebec (1929 Detroit card) vs Montreal (1941 Blaine card). The UK list gives Montreal as the port contracted to land. Ship's master: "H. Sibbons" (book notes, full image) vs "R. GIBSON[?]" (our reading of the smaller copy). Spelling: "Laurence" on the UK outward list; "Lawrence" on every U.S. form. Street: "Greive St." on the UK outward list; "Grieve St." on the U.S. manifest and Detroit card. Last foreign residence: Dunfermline on every 1929 form; "Ayr, Scotland" on the 1943 petition. Height: 6 ft (1929 card and manifest) vs 5 ft 11 in (1943 petition). 3. The ship Name Duchess of Bedford; renamed Empress of France in 1947 [1] Owner / operator Canadian Pacific Railway Co. (Canadian Pacific Steamships, managers) [2] Official number 160482 [2] — the same number written on the 1929 outward list Signal letters G N T V [2] Builder John Brown & Co., Clydebank, yard no. 518 [1] [2] Launched 24 January 1928, by Mrs. Stanley Baldwin, wife of the Prime Minister [2] . One source gives 25 January [3] . Completed / maiden voyage Completed May 1928 [1] ; maiden voyage Liverpool–Quebec–Montreal, 1 June 1928 [2] [3] Tonnage 20,123 gross [1] [3] [4] ; 20,448 gross, 11,335 net in a later register [2] Size 581.9 ft registered length, 75.2 ft breadth [2] [4] ; about 601 ft overall [1] [3] Engines / speed Steam turbines, twin screws, 18 knots [1] [3] Look Two masts, two funnels [3] Passengers as built 580 cabin, 480 tourist, 510 third; crew 510 [1] Cabins All cabins had hot and cold running water [1] Nickname The four sisters were called the "Drunken Duchesses" for their tendency to roll [1] Sisters Duchess of Atholl, Duchess of Richmond, Duchess of York [1] [3] Usual route Liverpool to Quebec and Montreal via Belfast and Greenock (as printed on Duchess of Bedford passenger lists of 1931–1932) [3] . Built to go up the St. Lawrence past Quebec to Montreal so passengers could go on by train to Chicago and the Midwest [1] . 4. Inside the ship, 1928 Dining saloon on A Deck, looking aft. © Crown copyright, National Records of Scotland, UCS1/116/31/16, IMGAAA00564. Drawing and Observation Room on the Promenade Deck, looking toward the port side. © Crown copyright, National Records of Scotland, UCS1/116/31/3, IMGAAA00561. Cabin No. 103, three berths, A Deck. © Crown copyright, National Records of Scotland, UCS1/116/31/22, IMGAAA00565. This is not known to be their cabin. Printed material from Canadian Pacific These are Canadian Pacific's own advertising and passenger papers for the Duchess ships. None of them is from Laurence and Janet's own sailing. Canadian Pacific advertisement, The Mitre, November 1928, page 14: "Duchess Cruises to the West Indies" on the Duchess of Bedford, from $200. These are winter cruise prices from New York, not the 1929 Atlantic fare. Scan: Bishop's University. Full page and text . "Canadian Pacific · The Duchesses," passenger booklet cover from a Duchess of Bedford sailing of 4 September 1931. Digitized by GG Archives. Document page . Canadian Pacific Atlantic Track Chart, with a table of approximate distances and a blank log for the ship's daily position. From the same 1931 material. Digitized by GG Archives. Document page . 5. The rules they travelled under U.S. Immigration Act of 1924: each immigrant needed a consular immigration visa stating whether he was a quota immigrant (section 5) or non-quota (section 4); fee $9 per visa [10] . Lawrence's card reads "Sec 5." Head tax: $8 per immigrant, set by the Act of 1917 [11] . New quotas took effect July 1, 1929 — two months before he sailed. Great Britain and Northern Ireland: 65,721 a year [9] , up from 34,007. From May to October 1929 the UK recorded 2,345 (May), 1,329 (June) and 1,562 (July) British subjects leaving to live in the U.S. [12] Arrivals at Detroit from Canada were recorded on card manifests; the Detroit cards are NARA microfilm M1478 [13] . 6. The rail leg His 1943 petition says he came into the U.S. at Detroit "on the C. P. R. R." (Canadian Pacific Railway). Canadian Pacific and the Michigan Central ran a pooled through train, the Canadian, Montreal–Toronto–Detroit–Chicago, using the Michigan Central tunnel under the Detroit River (opened 1910) [14] . Which train he took is not recorded. 7. Fares (not his fare) One source gives Cabin Class on a Duchess at $157.50 and Third Class at $87.50, Canada–England, one way; that source does not give the year [8] . Canadian Pacific fare sheets of the period survive in the UBC Chung Collection, including a tourist third cabin fare list dated March 1, 1929 [7] , and deck plans of the Duchesses dated Dec. 1928, Apr. 1929 and Jul. 1929 [6] . What Laurence and Janet paid, who bought the tickets, and their cabin numbers: not in any document held. 8. Still unknown Ticket numbers 32480 and 33082 need re-checking on the full original image. Cabin and berth; fare; payer beyond "Self." Janet's money shown. Whether the ship called at Liverpool and Belfast before Greenock on this sailing. Certificate of Arrival 3-234422. Which train, and the date and time they left Quebec. t: The Case for Sir Nathaniel Dunlop
x: The man at Shieldhill Nathaniel Dunlop was born at Campbeltown on April 7, 1830. He spent half a century with the Allan Line, the Glasgow shipping company whose steamers carried tens of thousands of Scots to Canada, became senior partner of its firm, James & Alexander Allan, and chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust. His wife died within weeks of the birth of their only child, Ellen, and he never remarried. In 1898 he bought Shieldhill, near Biggar, from the Chancellor family, who had held it since 1434, and with it the village of Quothquan below the house and its cottages. When he died at Shieldhill in 1919, his will left his daughter alone £100,000. A home, a hall, and a village “Domestic servant” is what Agnes Brown wrote when she registered her son. The same record gives her usual home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill. Those are two different pieces of information. The entry leaves her employer unnamed. It gives us no basis for placing her at work in the mansion, identifying who paid her wages, or saying she attended a particular gathering. Three places matter. Shieldhill House was the Dunlops’ private residence. A reported supper in its dining room brought tenants and servants there as invited guests. Shieldhill Hall was a separate building in Quothquan. Nathaniel and his daughter Ellen built it in 1903 for evening worship. It later housed winter lessons and a concert. Gean Cottage was the address Agnes gave in 1907. The project’s comparison of modern coordinates puts the cottage about 400 feet from the hall in a straight line. The mansion was farther away. The same household could invite a villager to worship, provide a room for a class, and receive her socially. Nathaniel also owned houses in the village. A May 1906 water-supply report establishes that much. The account cited here does not name Gean Cottage. A valuation roll or rental naming its proprietor and occupier would answer the narrower question. Laurence’s civil birth entry · Historic Environment Scotland, LB12995 · Motherwell Times, May 4, 1906 · Estate and newspaper research notes Who was actually there? January 1, 1902 Supper and dancing inside Shieldhill House The Hamilton Advertiser named Mr and Miss Dunlop as hosts. Tenants, villagers, estate servants and house servants came to supper and a dance in the mansion. The paper described supper in the dining room. It is direct evidence that the owners opened their private house across employment and social lines on this occasion. Agnes would have been sixteen. The report gives no evidence that she danced there or that this happened every year. Hamilton Advertiser, January 4, 1902, page 6 December 1905 A lecture and Christmas party in the hall The newspaper attributed the invitation for the lecture to father and daughter and reported a Christmas party in the hall. The named invitation establishes sponsorship. It cannot supply a guest list or put either host at every event. Hamilton Advertiser, December 30, 1905, page 6 March 9, 1906 A bowling club supper in the village schoolroom About seventy sat down to supper and a dance followed. The club organized the event. The report names the Rev. Mr Picken and local musicians. It names neither Dunlop nor Agnes. This is an important comparison: Quothquan also had gatherings organized outside the mansion and the Dunlops’ hall. Hamilton Advertiser, March 17, 1906, page 6 · Issue reference July 11, 1906 From Biggar to the hall, then to Shieldhill This is the closest dated evidence presented here for Nathaniel at an estate gathering before the estimated autumn conception. More than seventy members and associates of the Biggar and Culter branch of the Scotch Girls’ Friendly Society travelled from Biggar. Ellen met them at Quothquan. The Rev. C. Ross Lowdon conducted the service. The visitors went on to Shieldhill, gathered for tea at half past four and enjoyed the gardens and pond. The paper specifically describes Mr Dunlop arriving from the city and welcoming them. Ellen organized the visit. Nathaniel’s reported arrival places him there for part of it. The clipping lists neither Agnes nor Binnie. It supplies no evidence of a private meeting. Hamilton Advertiser, July 21, 1906, page 5 · Issue reference Hamilton Advertiser, July 21, 1906, page 5. "Mr Dunlop, on his arrival from the city, gave a cordial welcome to all." (British Newspaper Archive) Winter 1906–07 Lessons and the closing concert The April 6 report describes a teacher coming from Glasgow twice a week, music lessons and farm servants learning to read music. At the closing concert, Nathaniel chaired and Ellen played the piano. About two hundred people attended. The report places the owner publicly at the hall during Agnes’s pregnancy. It cannot identify where he was on a particular day the preceding autumn. Hamilton Advertiser, April 6, 1907, page 6 March 29, 1910 A crowded hall, three years after the birth The report names Sir Nathaniel in the chair, W. F. Addie as violin teacher, Miss Reid as a singer and Mrs M’Lellan in connection with needlework. The activities outlasted the period of the pregnancy. They also depended on teachers, clergy, performers and families whose names survive alongside those of the owners. Hamilton Advertiser, April 2, 1910, page 6 · Issue reference How much influence did one household have? Consider the July visit from a guest’s perspective as far as the report permits. The society assembled in Biggar. Ellen met the party, guided it to worship and hosted it at her family’s home. The minister led the service. The secretary reported on the society. Nathaniel arrived later. The distinction matters. The story preserves the authority of the landowner, the organizing work of his daughter, and the independent roles of the society and church. The evidence supports a concentrated form of estate patronage. The Dunlops supplied premises, extended invitations and presided at public occasions. People who might work on the estate could also encounter the family as neighbours, pupils, worshippers and guests. The newspapers give us the hosts’ public reputation. They tell us little about how a young servant experienced those relationships in private. There is no account here from Agnes describing pressure to attend, surveillance, punishment for staying away, control of courtship, or a demand for secrecy. No source cited here identifies Shieldhill as a cult. The records can support a precise question about social power: did access to housing, worship or assistance depend on maintaining the family’s favour? Tenancy terms, private correspondence, church minutes and testimony from residents would carry more weight on that point than newspaper praise. Historic Environment Scotland, LB12995 · Hamilton Advertiser, July 21, 1906, page 5 · Issue reference · Hamilton Advertiser, March 17, 1906, page 6 · Issue reference Nathaniel and Binnie, compared Presence. Nathaniel has an on-site sighting in July 1906. His absence from the start of the festival is part of that evidence, too. Binnie’s relationship to the owner is documented in census and family records. His 1907 medical entry gives 16 Carlton Place, Glasgow. His former school’s register, published in 1905, gives Charteris House, Woodford Green, Essex. Neither address fixes his daily movements. No dated source presented here places the nephew at Shieldhill in the relevant autumn. No dated source places either man together with Agnes. What the word “doctor” can mean. Binnie was a qualified medical practitioner before the pregnancy. Nathaniel received an honorary Doctor of Laws in April 1907. That distinction came after the estimated conception and before the birth. In June a newspaper used “Dr” for Nathaniel. If the family recollection specifically meant a practising physician, it points more naturally toward Binnie. If it preserved the title by which a man was known later, Nathaniel remains possible. Laurence’s daughter supplied a description, not either man’s name. Age, standing and opportunity. In autumn 1906 Agnes was twenty, Binnie thirty-two and Nathaniel about seventy-six. Nathaniel was a shipping executive with an estate and a public role. His position helps explain why his movements appear in newspapers. It does not establish a relationship or payment. Binnie may have left fewer public traces. Counting articles about one man and comparing that total with silence about the other would exaggerate the difference. Why Nathaniel leads. One man can be placed in the social setting itself, at a dated function in the relevant year. For the other, the chain stops at kinship, profession and addresses elsewhere. That is a defensible order for pursuing the two men. It gives no probability of paternity, and the identity of the father could lie outside the Dunlop family. Dunlop household, 1861 · Dr James Dunlop’s obituary · 1905 college register · 1907 Medical Register · Glasgow newspapers, April 1907 · Naval & Military Record, June 6, 1907 · The London Gazette, July 26, 1907 Follow Agnes through the records The neighbours. In 1901 Agnes lived with her uncle at Lime Tree Cottage. Mary Archibald, a sewing mistress, was recorded at Gean Tree Cottages. Mary’s brother Alexander, a domestic gardener, headed a household recorded at Shieldhill with his wife Annie and a servant. The census does not say which building the gardener occupied. Similar cottage names six years apart are a reason to track tenants. They do not establish that Mary and Agnes shared a household during the pregnancy. The birth. Agnes gave birth at nine in the evening on June 14, 1907, at the Royal Maternity Hospital in Edinburgh. She registered Lawrence Brown on July 4. The father’s entry is blank. Autumn 1906 is an estimate from the birth date. A gestational age or an earlier clinical entry could shift that estimate. A summer festival and a winter concert sit on either side of the period that matters most. Edinburgh. The electoral rolls list a Robert Douglas at 18 Lochrin Place around the time of the birth. In the 1911 census three-year-old Laurence was in the Douglas household at No. 16. Those are strong pieces of the child’s history. They leave the date of his move, the person who arranged his care, and the identity of his father unanswered. Likewise, Nathaniel’s reported appearances in Glasgow on June 21 and July 2, 1907 concern the registration period, months after the estimated conception. The family account. Laurence’s daughter, Constance Anderson Douglas, told her son that her father’s father was a doctor at the estate and that a gardener took him in. Her recollection is preserved in her own right as family testimony. The identification of a gardener and two possible meanings of “doctor” makes her account investigable. It does not establish who took custody of the baby or who fathered him. 1901 Libberton census · Alexander’s census entry · Laurence’s civil birth entry · Lochrin Place electoral roll · 1911 Douglas household · Family testimony, maps and weather What would change the finding? A record from autumn 1906. The first target is a dated household diary, letter, guest book, estate account or local report placing either man and Agnes at the same address in approximately August–October. A long absence documented across that period would weaken that man’s case. A shared event would establish an opportunity to meet. A private letter acknowledging a child would carry much greater weight. An address with a name attached. The 1905–06 and 1906–07 valuation rolls and any surviving rent book could identify the owner and tenant of Gean Cottage. A wage book or hiring agreement naming Agnes could identify her employer. The two records would answer different questions. Class registers or festival membership lists could settle whether she attended. Even proof of attendance would leave the identity of the father open. Acknowledgment or support. A later correction to the birth entry, a sheriff-court aliment action for child support, or a parish relief application could name a man and state who supplied the information. A claim by the mother, an acknowledgment by a man and a court finding carry different evidential weight. Hospital registers and casebooks for June and July 1907 may reveal admission, discharge or a contact. Their usefulness does not depend on naming the father. Family DNA. A match to relatives shared by uncle and nephew could support a Dunlop connection while leaving the individual unresolved. Documented descendants of different branches, multiple independent matches and the ability to account for other shared ancestors would matter. Until a record or a discriminating set of matches links an individual to this child, Laurence’s biological father remains unidentified. x: ← Cold Case File The Names He Carried Item 101 · March 16, 1901 Obituary: James Dunlop, Campbeltown Courier Source: Campbeltown Courier, Saturday, March 16, 1901, page 3, “Death of Professor James Dunlop.” British Newspaper Archive, article 090. Report reference BNA-006. The original Open the original page in the British Newspaper Archive (sign-in needed). Source of the reading: British Newspaper Archive research report, November 25, 2026 (PDF) . Transcription, word for word The whole obituary, read from the page image. Paragraph breaks are not all kept. Line breaks and printer’s hyphens are joined up. Death of Professor James Dunlop. Our readers will learn with much regret of the death of Professor James Dunlop, M.D., which took place at his residence, Carlton Place, Glasgow, on Wednesday morning. Dr Dunlop had been in failing health for some years, and latterly it had been apparent to his friends that the weakness from which he suffered was gradually increasing. Last week unfavourable symptoms appeared, but immediate danger was not apprehended, and the end came somewhat suddenly. Dr Dunlop, who was 67 years of age, was a native of Campbeltown. He was educated at the Grammar School here, and about half a century ago, with his brothers Archibald, Nathaniel, and Matthew, went to Glasgow. While the three elder brothers went into business—in which each in his own sphere became well known—James entered Glasgow University, then in the old building in the High Street. There he had a distinguished career, carrying off numerous prizes. In 1857 he took the degree of M.D., and a year later became a Licentiate of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons. Immediately on graduation he received an appointment as one of the assistants in the Royal Infirmary, where he had the advantage of working under Dr Joseph, now Lord, Lister. The special bent of his studies had been in the direction of surgery, and a vacancy occurring in Anderson's College through the transference of Sir George MacLeod to the Chair of Surgery in the University, notwithstanding his youth and comparatively limited experience Dr Dunlop became a candidate. He was well supported by Dr Lister and others, who knew and could appreciate his ability, and was duly elected to the professorship, holding the office for about twenty years.
