t: Dr. Binnie Dunlop (1874–1946)
x: ← The Names He Carried Cold Case File Research File The Dunlops Dr. Binnie Dunlop (1874–1946) Nephew of Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill · son of Dr. James Dunlop · one of the two men examined in the Cold Case File Binnie Dunlop was born on August 3, 1874, to Dr. James Dunlop and Jane Menzies Binnie, and qualified in medicine at the University of Glasgow (M.B., 1898). He was Sir Nathaniel Dunlop’s nephew. Because the family remembered Laurence’s father as a doctor, Binnie is one of the two men the Cold Case File examines. No record yet places him at Shieldhill or near Agnes. Eugenics and the Malthusian League Binnie Dunlop never practised as a doctor. He gave his life to the population question. He joined the Malthusian League in 1910 and served as its honorary secretary and treasurer, and he edited its paper, The Malthusian , from 1918 to 1921. He was probably the anonymous author of the League’s 1913 pamphlet on birth control. Reference works describe him as an advocate of eugenics, and his obituary appeared in the Eugenics Review in October 1946. His own published letters show what he believed. In them he wrote: “Although the poor and the unfit continued ‘propagating their kind unchecked’… Hence the reversed selection which you rightly deplore.” (January 1913) “…they bring into the world several times that number, half of whom grow up more or less defective, and half of whom die prematurely.” (January 1913) “It seems to me most urgent—on humanitarian, eugenic, and social-unrest grounds… that we immediately begin to encourage the married poor to avoid bringing more children into the world…” (September 1913) “…doctors and nurses must realise that it is dysgenic, as well as cruel, to leave parents ignorant of family limitation…” (February 1914) “…the extending of this knowledge to the wage-earners… is—on humanitarian, eugenic, and anti-socialistic grounds—by far the most urgently needed reform of the day.” (April 1914) Each quotation is from the full letter, transcribed word for word, in the Cold Case File below. t: Dr. James Dunlop (about 1834–1901)
x: ← The Names He Carried Cold Case File Research File The Dunlops Dr. James Dunlop, M.D. (about 1834–1901) Brother of Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill · father of Dr. Binnie Dunlop James Dunlop was a Glasgow doctor born in Kintyre, near Campbeltown. He was Sir Nathaniel Dunlop’s brother and Binnie Dunlop’s father. He died at his home, 16 Carlton Place, Glasgow, on Wednesday, March 13, 1901, aged 67. The brothers His obituary in the Campbeltown Courier of March 16, 1901 says he went to Glasgow “with his brothers Archibald, Nathaniel, and Matthew.” The three older brothers went into business, and James entered Glasgow University. This is a newspaper of the time naming Nathaniel as his brother, in so many words. His life and work His hometown paper, the Campbeltown Courier , called him Professor James Dunlop. He went to Campbeltown Grammar School, took his M.D. at Glasgow in 1857, and worked at the Glasgow Royal Infirmary under Joseph Lister. He held the professorship of surgery at Anderson’s College for about twenty years and was a surgeon of the Royal Infirmary for forty. He was Medico-Legal Adviser to the Crown in Glasgow’s great criminal trials, surgeon of the Lock Hospital, a governor of the Samaritan and Victoria hospitals, and consulting surgeon to the Caledonian Railway and the Clyde Pilot Board. He pushed for vaccination and isolation in a smallpox epidemic, and was a volunteer officer for forty years with the 3rd Lanark Rifle Volunteers, rising to Brigade-Surgeon-Lieutenant-Colonel. At 67 he volunteered for the South African War. In January 1900 he sailed as acting surgeon on the troopship Bavaria, paying his own way, and worked six to seven months in the surgical wards of the Wynberg Base Hospital near Cape Town. The Glasgow Medical Journal obituary (April 1901) calls him one of the busiest men in the city, with many public posts and a large private practice, until failing health made him cut back. He was admitted a Fellow of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons on June 4, 1860, and spent his whole working life in Glasgow. In his spare time he studied the natural history of deep-sea fish on his yearly visits to Kintyre, writing on them in the Glasgow Herald, and he lectured on ancient Egypt. His published papers included notes on post-mortem examinations in criminal cases for the Crown in Glasgow (1893) and an address on the Victoria Infirmary (1896). Dear Mr. Rankin, I have completed the reading of the History of your firm, and now have the pleasure of returning the book to its owner. I gave the leisure of the whole time since it came, to its perusal, and I think I may claim to have had more enjoyment in it than any other reader, apart from yourselves, is likely to have had. This because, when I entered business over 60 years ago, I was placed in the midst of your firm's business activities; I was acquainted with some of its leading members, and familiar, too, with much of its history. It has been like living again through that wonderful period of my young life when so many great chiefs of industry filled the ground around, and the future was full of promise. I have nothing really to add to or take away from the story you have told. It was a wonderful time when men from Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, and Argyllshire—all mostly of the same stock—men with big heads, full of courage and enterprise, abounding energy, and the highest integrity, went out into the fields of foreign trade that were waiting to be opened up, founded great industries, and spread themselves out in every direction. Among these were not only those of whom you write—the Gilmours, Polloks, and Rankins, with their immediate relatives and friends—but there were the Allans, who founded the business with which I am connected, establishing themselves in Canada as pioneers; the Gillespies from this neighbourhood, who founded the Gillespie-Moffat firms of London and Canada, and the timber-trading houses of Quebec which bore their name. There were the Patersons and the Greenshields from Ayrshire, the Smiths and Workmans who first in Ireland opened up the linen trade, and later became great ware

OBITUARY Sir Nathaniel Dunlop Steamboat Man, Is Dead LONDON, Nov. 16.—The death is announced of Sir Nathaniel Dunlop. Sir Nathaniel Dunlop was a retired ship owner and formerly chairman of the Allan line steamship company. He was considered responsible for the introduction of the steam turbine engine in ocean going vessels. He was born in 1830, was a widower, and is survived by one daughter. t: Miss Ellen Smith Dunlop (1867–1958)
x: ← The Names He Carried Cold Case File Research File The Dunlops Miss Ellen Smith Dunlop (1867–1958) Only child of Sir Nathaniel Dunlop · of Shieldhill, Quothquan · never married Portrait of Ellen Smith Dunlop. Photograph supplied by Doug Garceau, November 25, 2026. The photographer and date are not recorded. A portrait of her is also in the Charlie Todd Collection on the Quothquan and Thankerton Community Council website. Ellen Smith Dunlop was the only child of Nathaniel Dunlop and his wife Ellen Smith, who died soon after her birth in 1867. Her father never remarried. From 1898 she lived with him at Shieldhill, the estate above the village of Quothquan, and she stayed there for the rest of her life. Her work in Quothquan The newspapers show Ellen as the working hand behind the family’s life in the village. Date What the record says Source December 1900 Miss Dunlop pays for the Quothquan Christmas party. Hamilton Advertiser, December 29, 1900 1903 She and her father build Shieldhill Hall in Quothquan for evening worship, about 400 feet from Gean Cottage. Historic Environment Scotland, LB12995 July 11, 1906 She organizes the Scotch Girls’ Friendly Society visit, meets the party at Quothquan and hosts it at Shieldhill. Hamilton Advertiser, July 21, 1906 Winter 1906–07 At the closing concert of the hall’s winter classes, her father chairs and she plays the piano. Hamilton Advertiser, April 6, 1907 1911 She finances the Thankerton Creamery, opened that year. Quothquan and Thankerton Community Council, Historical Photographs November 1918 A Women’s Rural Institute is formed in Shieldhill Hall. Hamilton Advertiser, November 16, 1918, page 5 1940 She shows Highland cattle under the herd name “of Quothquan.” Transactions of the Highland and Agricultural Society (1940) Her father’s death and her own Sir Nathaniel died at Shieldhill in 1919. The Chicago Daily Tribune reported that he “is survived by one daughter.” His will named her first among his heirs and left her alone £100,000. She kept Shieldhill until her death in 1958. The community council’s history says she left most of her estate to her staff, including her maid and companion of fifty years, and to local charities, and Shieldhill Hall to the Church of Scotland.
